Semmelweis was puzzled that puerperal fever was rare among women giving street births [...] Semmelweis' breakthrough occurred in 1847, following the death of his good friend Jakob Kolletschka, who had been accidentally poked with a student's scalpel while performing a post mortem examination. Kolletschka's autopsy showed a pathology similar to that of the women who were dying from puerperal fever. [...] He proposed that he and the medical students carried "cadaverous particles" on their hands from the autopsy room to the patients they examined in the First Obstetrical Clinic. This explained why the student midwives in the Second Clinic, who were not engaged in autopsies and had no contact with corpses, saw a much lower mortality rate. [...] He instituted a policy of using a solution of chlorinated lime (calcium hypochlorite) for washing hands between autopsy work and the examination of patients. [...] The mortality rate in April 1847, before the new hand washing procedures were instituted, was 18.3%. The new procedures started in mid-May leading to lower rates:  June 2.2%, July 1.2%, and August 1.9%. [...] Semmelweis's hypothesis, that there was only one cause, that the primary factor was cleanliness, was extreme at the time and was largely ignored, rejected, or ridiculed. [...] Some doctors, for instance, were offended at the suggestion that they should wash their hands, feeling that their social status as gentlemen was inconsistent with the idea that their hands could be unclean. [...] He died after two weeks, on 13 August 1865, aged 47, from a gangrenous wound, due to an infection on his right hand which might have been caused by the struggle. [...] In the asylum, he was beaten by the guards. He died 14 days later from a gangrenous wound on his right hand that may have been caused by the beating. Semmelweis's findings only gained widespread acceptance years after his death, when Louis Pasteur confirmed the germ theory of disease, giving Semmelweis's observations a scientific explanation

gancho: Mary Mallon, a "Maria Tifoide", se sentia saudável, mas espalhou febre tifoide como cozinheira em Nova York. Foi confinada numa ilha de 1915 até morrer, em 1938. Outros portadores tiveram tratamento mais brando.
explicacao: Imigrante irlandesa, Mallon cozinhava para famílias ricas de Nova York. Em 1906, depois de um surto de febre tifoide numa casa de veraneio em Oyster Bay, o dono do imóvel contratou George Soper, engenheiro sanitário e epidemiologista, para achar a causa. Soper viu que ela tinha trabalhado para oito famílias, sete delas com casos da doença. Como cozinhar mata a bactéria, ele estranhou, até saber que ela servia um sorvete com pêssegos frescos. Soper conhecia a ideia de portadores assintomáticos, gente infectada sem nenhum sinal da doença. Mallon, que não acreditava estar infectada, o recebeu empunhando um garfo de trinchar, e depois resistiu à polícia. Os exames acharam o bacilo nas fezes dela, e em 1907 ela foi levada a um hospital de isolamento na ilha North Brother. Solta em 1910, com a promessa de não trabalhar mais como cozinheira, foi contratada em 1914, com o nome de Mary Brown, por uma maternidade, que no início de 1915 teve um surto com 25 casos e duas mortes. Ela voltou à ilha e lá ficou até morrer. O caso ainda levanta questões éticas: durante o confinamento dela, foram identificados outros 400 portadores sem sintomas, e nenhum ficou isolado por tanto tempo; alguns, que trabalhavam com comida, ganharam emprego e aluguel pagos pelo Estado.

fontes.trecho: was an Irish-born cook who lived in the United States from a young age and is believed to have infected up to fifty-seven people with the bacteria that cause typhoid fever. [...] She was the first person in the U.S. to be identified as an asymptomatic carrier of Salmonella typhi bacteria. [...] In 1907, she was forcibly quarantined at the Riverside Hospital, an institution for those with quarantinable diseases, on North Brother Island in New York City's East River. She was released in 1910 after she swore to report to the health department every quarter and not return to cooking as a career. A further typhoid outbreak at the Sloane Maternity Hospital in early 1915 resulted in twenty-five cases and two deaths. Mallon was identified as the responsible party and was returned to North Brother Island. She remained there until her death in 1938. [...] Mallon's case raises ethical questions about the balance between protection of individual liberty and the requirements of public health. She was treated differently from the four hundred other asymptomatic typhoid carriers identified during her confinement. Others who worked in the food industry were given jobs and had their rents paid for by the state, and none were confined for the same length of time as she was. [...] Mallon was soon employed as a private cook with a series of wealthy New York families [...] Mallon worked as a cook for Charles Henry Warren, a New York banker in 1906. He and his family spent the summer that year at Oyster Bay on the North Shore of Long Island, where they had rented a house from George Thompson. [...] he hired George Soper, a sanitation engineer and epidemiologist for the New York Department of Health, to investigate the source of the problem. [...] At first, he was unsure whether a cook could be the source, since cooking would kill the bacteria; he became more convinced, however, when he learned that Mallon prepared an ice cream dessert with fresh peaches. [...] He saw she had worked for eight families, seven of whom had suffered typhoid outbreaks. [...] Soper was aware of the existence of asymptomatic carriers—carriers that are infected with a pathogen, but show no signs or symptoms [...] It did not take Mary long to react to this suggestion. She seized a carving fork and advanced in my direction. [...] Mallon's refusal was based on her belief that she was not infected. [...] Her stools were tested three times a week and showed the presence of Bacillus typhosus. [...] the earliest confirmed instance of Mallon being employed as a cook after her release from North Brother Island was in October 1914, when she was hired under the name Mary Brown by the Sloane Maternity Hospital.

gancho: Em 1881, um médico cubano propôs que a febre amarela era transmitida por mosquitos e foi alvo de zombaria. Em 1900, a ideia foi confirmada, e um dos pesquisadores morreu depois de se deixar picar.
explicacao: Carlos Finlay, nascido em Cuba em 1833, defendeu na Conferência Sanitária Internacional de 1881 que um mosquito que picasse um doente de febre amarela poderia, depois, infectar uma pessoa sadia. A ideia foi mal recebida e motivo de deboche. No ano seguinte, ele apontou um mosquito do gênero Aedes como o transmissor e recomendou controlar a população do inseto. Quase vinte anos depois, em 1900, a Comissão Walter Reed, do Exército americano, confirmou a hipótese. Um de seus membros, o médico Jesse Lazear, era o único com experiência com mosquitos e usou larvas do laboratório de Finlay. Ele deixou de propósito que um mosquito infectado o picasse, para estudar a doença. Adoeceu e morreu aos 34 anos, dezessete dias depois de escrever à mulher que achava estar na pista do "germe verdadeiro". Na época, a versão divulgada foi a de que ele tinha confundido o mosquito com um inofensivo; o caráter deliberado só veio à tona em 1947, no caderno do próprio Lazear. Reed deu a Finlay o crédito pela descoberta do transmissor. O cubano foi indicado sete vezes ao Nobel de Medicina e nunca ganhou.

fontes.trecho: Carlos Juan Finlay (December 3, 1833 – August 20, 1915) was a Cuban epidemiologist [...] He was the first to theorize, in 1881, that a mosquito was a carrier, now known as a disease vector, of the organism causing yellow fever: a mosquito that bites a victim of the disease could subsequently bite and thereby infect a healthy person. He presented this theory at the 1881 International Sanitary Conference, where it was not well-received, and in fact made him subject to ridicule and mockery.  A year later Finlay identified a mosquito of the genus Aedes as the organism transmitting yellow fever. His theory was followed by the recommendation to control the mosquito population as a way to control the spread of the disease. His hypothesis and exhaustive proofs were confirmed nearly twenty years later by the Walter Reed Commission of 1900. [...] Reed himself credited Finlay with the discovery of the yellow fever vector [...] Finlay was nominated seven times for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, although he was never awarded the prize.

In 1900 he reported for duty as the assistant surgeon at Columbia Barracks (Quemados, Cuba) for the United States Army. [...] Lazear was the only member of the commission who had experience working with mosquitoes, and he used mosquito larvae from Finlay's laboratory. He wrote to his wife in a letter dated September 8, 1900, "I rather think I am on the track of the real germ." Lazear deliberately allowed an infected mosquito to bite him in order to study the disease. He contracted the disease and died at age 34, seventeen days after writing his hopeful letter. The fact that this was a deliberate act was covered up at the time—for reasons unknown, but possibly connected with family insurance policies—and the story put about that Lazear had mistaken the mosquito for an uninfected one of a different species. The truth was discovered in 1947 by Philip S. Hench from Lazear's own notebook.

gancho: Na obra do Canal do Panamá, o chefe da comissão pediu a Theodore Roosevelt que afastasse o médico por sua obsessão cara com mosquitos. Roosevelt manteve o médico, e a febre amarela quase sumiu da zona do canal.
explicacao: Quando os EUA assumiram o projeto, em 1904, o istmo do Panamá era famoso pelas doenças tropicais: estima-se que mais de 22 mil trabalhadores tinham morrido durante a tentativa francesa de abrir o canal. Por muito tempo se acreditou que a febre amarela vinha da sujeira e a malária de vapores nocivos, mas pesquisas feitas entre 1897 e 1902 mostraram que as duas eram espalhadas por mosquitos. O coronel William Gorgas, chefe de saneamento, montou uma guerra contra eles: inspetores procuravam larvas de casa em casa, a água parada era eliminada ou coberta com óleo, pântanos foram drenados e todos os prédios foram fumigados. A "teoria do mosquito" ainda era vista como controversa, e o custo era alto. Theodore Shonts, chefe da comissão do canal, pediu a Roosevelt que tirasse Gorgas do projeto. O presidente consultou dois médicos de renome e ouviu que teria o canal se ficasse com Gorgas. Deu a ele apoio total. Em 1906, houve um único caso de febre amarela, e as mortes por malária também caíram muito. A proteção, porém, foi desigual: os trabalhadores negros, a maioria da mão de obra, muitas vezes moravam fora da área controlada e, em 1906, morriam a uma taxa dez vezes maior que a dos brancos. No total, morreram 350 trabalhadores brancos e 4.500 negros, bem menos que na época francesa.

fontes.titulo: Health measures during the construction of the Panama Canal
fontes.trecho: By the time the United States took control of the Panama Canal project on May 4, 1904, the Isthmus of Panama was notorious for tropical diseases. An estimated 12,000 workers had died during the construction of the Panama Railway and over 22,000 during the French effort to build a canal. [...] Traditionally, yellow fever had been thought to be caused by contact with filth and malaria by noxious vapors. However, between 1897 and 1902, both diseases were shown to be spread by mosquitoes [...] The Panama Canal Commission appointed Colonel William Crawford Gorgas in March 1904 as head of hospitals and sanitation. [...] There was initially considerable resistance to this program, as the "mosquito theory" was still considered controversial and unproven. [...] In each district, inspectors searched houses and buildings for mosquito larvae. [...] by eliminating standing water where possible and by spreading oil on the surface of any remaining pools, the larvae could be destroyed. [...] Gorgas organized a major program to drain and fill swamps and wetlands around the Canal Zone. [...] Within a year of Stevens's appointment, every building in Panama had been fumigated [...] In 1906, only one case of yellow fever was reported, and by the end of the Panama Canal's construction, there were zero every year. [...] Gorgas continuously faced opposition because of the cost- and manpower-intensive nature of the eradication work, as well as entrenched ideas that mosquitoes were irrelevant to disease spread. At one stage, Theodore P. Shonts, head of the commission responsible for the canal, requested U.S. President Theodore Roosevelt to remove Gorgas from the project because of his costly obsession with mosquitoes. Roosevelt asked advice from two leading physicians in the U.S. He was told that he had a choice between Shonts and Gorgas, and that he would get his canal if he supported Gorgas. Thereafter, Roosevelt gave Gorgas his full backing. In the end, these efforts were a success: by 1906, yellow fever was virtually wiped out in the Canal Zone, and the number of deaths caused by the other tropical disease, malaria, was also reduced significantly. [...] While disease reduction dramatically improved the health of white workers, black workers—the majority of the canal workforce—continued to die in large numbers, at ten times the rate of white workers in 1906. While medical care was provided to all, housing was not provided to workers, many of whom had to live in tents and tenements outside the mosquito-controlled zone. In the end, 350 white workers and 4,500 black workers had died. While the loss was tragic, it was far less than during the French era.

gancho: Em 1986, o verme-da-guiné infectava cerca de 3,5 milhões de pessoas por ano. Em 2025, foram 10 casos. E a doença está quase erradicada sem vacina nem remédio: com filtros de pano para a água e educação.
explicacao: A dracunculíase é causada por um verme que entra no corpo quando a pessoa bebe água com pequenos crustáceos, os copépodes, que carregam as larvas. Cerca de um ano depois, a fêmea adulta chega a um ponto de saída, em geral na perna, e forma uma bolha muito dolorosa. O verme sai pela ferida aos poucos, ao longo de semanas. Para aliviar a dor, o doente mergulha a perna na água, e é aí que o verme libera novas larvas, fechando o ciclo. Não existe medicamento para tratar nem para prevenir a doença: o tratamento ainda é enrolar o verme num pauzinho, alguns centímetros por dia. A campanha de erradicação começou nos anos 1980, depois do sucesso contra a varíola, e se apoia em medidas simples: filtros de náilon ou de pano fino que retêm os copépodes, educação de aldeia em aldeia para ninguém mergulhar feridas em fontes de água de beber e vigilância de cada caso. Os casos humanos caíram de cerca de 3,5 milhões por ano em 1986 para 10 em 2025, sobretudo no Chade, na Etiópia e no Sudão do Sul. Um obstáculo inesperado são os cães, que também se infectam e ajudaram a reacender a transmissão no Chade em 2010. Se a campanha der certo, esta será a segunda doença humana erradicada, depois da varíola.

fontes.trecho: A person becomes infected by drinking water contaminated with larvae that reside inside copepods (a type of small crustacean). [...] Around a year later, the adult female worm migrates to an exit site — usually the lower leg — and induces an intensely painful blister on the skin. Eventually, the blister bursts, creating a painful wound from which the worm gradually emerges over several weeks. [...] The female worm releases larvae when the host submerges the wound in water in attempts to relieve the pain, thus continuing the life cycle. There is no medication to treat or prevent dracunculiasis. Instead, the mainstay of treatment is the careful wrapping of the emerging worm around a small stick or gauz to encourage and speed up its exit. Each day, a few more centimeters of the worm emerge [...] Prevention efforts center on filtering drinking water to remove copepods as well as public education campaigns to discourage people from soaking affected limbs in sources of drinking water [...] The effort to eradicate dracunculiasis began in the 1980s following the successful eradication of smallpox in 1977. [...] Dracunculiasis has become rare, with 10–15 human cases reported worldwide per year (15 in 2021, 13 in 2022, 14 in 2023, 15 in 2024, and 10 in 2025). This is down from 27 cases in 2020 and dramatically less than the estimated 3.5 million annual cases in 20 countries in 1986 [...] Dracunculiasis remains endemic primarily in three countries –  Chad, Ethiopia and South Sudan. [...] Nylon filters, finely woven cloth, or specialized filter straws can all remove copepods from drinking water, eliminating transmission risk. [...] The second phase involved the training and distribution of staff and volunteers to provide public education village-by-village, surveil for cases, and deliver water filters. [...] Infections of domestic dogs have been particularly common in Chad, where they helped reignite dracunculiasis transmission in 2010. [...] If the eradication program succeeds, dracunculiasis is expected to become the second human disease to be eradicated, after smallpox.

gancho: A segunda doença erradicada pela humanidade não era de gente: a peste bovina, declarada erradicada em 2011. Nos anos 1890, matou até 90% do gado do leste e do sul da África, e a fome pode ter levado um terço da Etiópia.
explicacao: A peste bovina, ou rinderpest ("peste do gado", em alemão), era causada por um vírus que atacava o gado, parente mais próximo do vírus do sarampo. No fim do século XIX, uma epidemia varreu a África e, segundo as estimativas, matou de 80% a 90% de todo o gado do leste e do sul do continente. Para povos que dependiam do pastoreio, da caça e da agricultura, o resultado foi fome em massa. Estima-se que as mortes humanas chegaram a um terço da população da Etiópia e a dois terços do povo massai da Tanzânia. O despovoamento teve um efeito em cadeia na paisagem: arbustos espinhosos tomaram as terras, criando o hábitat ideal para a mosca tsé-tsé, que transmite a doença do sono e torna a região imprópria para o gado. Depois de uma campanha mundial iniciada em meados do século XX, o último caso confirmado foi diagnosticado em 2001. Em 2010, a FAO, agência da ONU para alimentação e agricultura, anunciou o fim dos trabalhos de campo, e em junho de 2011 a erradicação global foi declarada oficialmente. Foi só a segunda doença da história a ser eliminada por completo, depois da varíola.

fontes.trecho: The term Rinderpest (German: [ˈʁɪndɐpɛst] ) is a German word meaning "cattle plague". Rinderpest virus (RPV) belongs to the genus Morbillivirus, alongside measles virus – its closest relative – and canine distemper virus. [...] After a global eradication campaign that began in the mid-20th century, the last confirmed case of rinderpest was diagnosed in 2001. In 2010, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) announced that field activities in the decades-long, worldwide campaign to eradicate the disease were ending, paving the way for a formal declaration in June 2011 of the global eradication of rinderpest. This makes it only the second disease in history to be fully wiped out, following smallpox. [...] The outbreak in the 1890s killed an estimated 80–90% of all cattle in eastern and southern Africa. [...] the consequent human toll was mass starvation in the absence of herding, hunting, and farming. The human losses were estimated to be as high as one-third of the population of Ethiopia and two-thirds of the Maasai people of Tanzania. This famine caused significant depopulation in sub-Saharan Africa, allowing thornbush to colonise. This formed ideal habitat for tsetse fly, which carries sleeping sickness and is unsuitable for livestock

gancho: O vírus do sarampo descende de um vírus de gado. Um estudo de 2020 estimou que os dois se separaram por volta do século VI a.C., quando surgiam cidades grandes o bastante para o sarampo circular sem parar.
explicacao: O parente mais próximo do vírus do sarampo é o da peste bovina, uma doença do gado hoje erradicada. Os dois descendem de um ancestral comum, muito provavelmente um vírus que infectava bois. Estimar quando se separaram é difícil: análises genéticas anteriores apontavam para os séculos XI e XII d.C., com margem que chegava ao século V d.C. Em 2020, um estudo sequenciou o genoma de um vírus de sarampo de 1912, recuperado de um pulmão conservado, e recalculou a separação para o século VI a.C., com média em 528 a.C. e um intervalo provável que vai de 1174 a.C. a 165 d.C. Essa época coincide com o surgimento das primeiras povoações humanas grandes o bastante para manter o sarampo circulando de forma contínua. A data marca a separação dos dois ramos: a passagem para humanos, e portanto o nascimento do sarampo como doença nossa, pode ter acontecido em qualquer ponto entre essa separação e o ancestral comum mais recente de todas as linhagens conhecidas, datado de 1880. Hoje, os humanos são os hospedeiros naturais do sarampo, e não se conhece nenhum reservatório animal.

fontes.trecho: The measles virus may have diverged from rinderpest around the 6th century BC, coinciding with the first human settlements large enough to sustain endemic measles transmission. [...] Measles virus and rinderpest virus diverged from a common ancestor, most likely a cattle-infecting virus. Earlier molecular clocks estimates have been superseded by a 2020 study, which sequenced the genome of a 1912 measles virus recovered from a preserved lung specimen and revised the estimated time of divergence to the 6th century BC (mean 528 BC, with a 95% credible interval of 1174 BC to 165 CE), coinciding with the rise of large cities. The spillover to humans; and thus the emergence of measles; could have occurred at any point between this divergence and the most recent common ancestor of all known measles virus strains, estimated at 1880 CE.

Humans are the natural hosts of the virus; no animal reservoirs are known to exist. [...] The measles virus evolved from the now eradicated rinderpest virus which infected cattle. Sequence analysis has suggested that the two viruses most probably diverged in the 11th and 12th centuries, though the periods as early as the 5th century fall within the 95% confidence interval of these calculations.

gancho: A máscara de bico, símbolo da peste, não é da Peste Negra nem da Idade Média: nada indica que tenha sido usada antes do século XVII. Alguns historiadores até defendem que a figura nasceu como ficção.
explicacao: O traje do "médico da peste" tinha chapéu de couro, máscara com olhos de vidro e um bico curvo, luvas, botas, túnica de linho encerado e uma vara para examinar os doentes sem tocar neles. O bico era recheado de coisas aromáticas, como flores secas, ervas, cânfora ou uma esponja com vinagre. A lógica vinha da teoria do miasma: um "ar ruim" seria a causa da doença, e os aromas protegeriam do mau cheiro. A teoria estava errada, mas o traje provavelmente protegia um pouco, porque cobria o corpo, e a túnica encerada impedia que as pulgas, as verdadeiras transmissoras da peste, se agarrassem ao tecido. A primeira descrição da roupa é atribuída a Charles de Lorme, médico do rei Luís XIII, durante um surto em Paris em 1619, com uma máscara de "nariz de meio pé" em forma de bico; pesquisas recentes, porém, pedem cautela com o relato dele. Um texto de 1373 já recomendava máscaras aos médicos, mas sem descrever como eram. A origem exata do traje é obscura, porque a maioria das imagens vem de textos satíricos e charges. Só se conhecem dois exemplares de máscara, ambos do século XVII e achados na Alemanha. A figura inspirou um personagem da commedia dell'arte e virou uma das máscaras típicas do Carnaval de Veneza.

fontes.trecho: Contrary to popular belief, no evidence suggests that the beak mask costume was worn during the Black Death or the Middle Ages. The costume started to appear in the 17th century when physicians studied and treated plague patients. [...] The costume consists of a leather hat, mask with glass eyes and a beak, stick to remove clothes of a plague victim, gloves, waxed linen robe, and boots. [...] The beak could hold dried flowers (commonly roses and carnations), herbs (commonly lavender and peppermint), camphor, or a vinegar sponge [...] The purpose of the mask was to keep away bad smells, such as the smell of decaying bodies. The smell taken with the most caution was known as miasma, a noxious form of "bad air." This was thought to be the principal cause of the disease. [...] Though these particular theories about the plague's nature were incorrect, it is likely that the costume actually did afford the wearer some protection. The garments covered the body, shielding against splattered blood, lymph, and cough droplets, and the waxed robe prevented fleas (the true carriers of the plague) from touching the body or clinging to the linen. [...] Doctors used wooden canes in order to point out areas needing attention and to examine patients without touching them. [...] The exact origins of the costume are unclear, as most depictions come from satirical writings and political cartoons. An early reference to plague doctors wearing masks is in 1373 when Johannes Jacobi recommends their use but he offers no physical description of what these masks looked like. [...] though some historians insist that the plague doctor was originally fictional and inspired the real plague doctors later. [...] The garments were first mentioned by a physician to King Louis XIII of France, Charles de Lorme, who wrote in a 1619 plague outbreak in Paris [...] De Lorme wrote that the mask had a "nose half a foot long, shaped like a beak, filled with perfume [...] Recent research has revealed that strong caveats must be applied with regard to De Lorme's assertions, however. [...] There are only two known artifacts of plague masks, both dated to the 17th century and both found in Germany. [...] The costume is also associated with a commedia dell'arte character called Il Medico della Peste ('The Plague Doctor'), who wears a distinctive plague doctor's mask. [...] is one of the distinctive masks worn during the Carnival of Venice.

gancho: Carlos Chagas achou primeiro um parasita novo no intestino do barbeiro e só depois foi atrás da doença. A partir de 1909, descreveu parasita, inseto vetor, hospedeiros e sintomas de uma doença até então desconhecida.
explicacao: Em 1907, Oswaldo Cruz mandou o jovem médico Carlos Chagas conter um surto de malária entre os trabalhadores de uma ferrovia em construção no interior de Minas Gerais. Acampado em Lassance, Chagas notou que as casas da roça estavam infestadas de um inseto grande que se alimenta de sangue, o barbeiro, chamado assim porque picava o rosto das pessoas à noite. Desconfiou na hora que ele pudesse transmitir algum parasita. No intestino dos insetos achou um protozoário de espécie nova, que batizou de Trypanosoma cruzi, em homenagem ao seu mentor, Oswaldo Cruz. Depois o encontrou no sangue de um gato e, em 14 de abril de 1909, no de Berenice, uma menina de dois anos que ele tinha visto na mesma casa onde o gato estivera. Em seguida, relacionou o parasita a lesões no coração e no cérebro, sugeriu o tatu como reservatório natural, descreveu 27 casos da forma aguda e fez mais de 100 autópsias de doentes crônicos. Ter descrito em detalhe uma doença desconhecida, com agente, vetor, hospedeiro, quadro clínico e epidemiologia, dá ao trabalho dele um lugar único na história da medicina. Chagas foi indicado ao Nobel em 1913 e em 1921, mas não ganhou. Muitos atribuem isso à oposição que ele sofreu no Brasil, onde houve quem duvidasse da existência da doença. A análise dos arquivos do Nobel, porém, aponta outros motivos: a cada vez ele teve um único indicador, brasileiro, e o comitê se ligava quase só a cientistas da Europa e dos EUA.

fontes.trecho: Chagas's work holds a unique place in the history of medicine, Chagas described in detail a previously-unknown infectious disease, its pathogen, vector (Triatominae), host, clinical manifestations, and epidemiology. [...] In 1907, there was an outbreak of malaria at the Minas Gerais hinterland, largely affecting railroad workers and greatly hampered the construction on new railway from Rio de Janeiro to the city of Belém in the Amazon. The Brazilian government asked Cruz for help. Cruz immediately assigned Chagas, with an assistant, Belisario Penna, to make the investigation. Camping at Lassance [...] During his investigation of malaria in Lassance, Chagas observed the peculiar infestation of the rural houses with a large hematophagous insect of the genus Triatoma, a kind of "assassin bug" or "kissing bug" (barbeiro, "barber" in Portuguese, so-called because it sucked the blood at night by biting the faces of its victims). [...] if by any chance it were, as I immediately supposed, a transmitter of any parasite of man or of another vertebrate. He discovered that the intestines of these insects harbored flagellate protozoans, a new species of the genus Trypanosoma [...] Chagas named this new parasite Trypanosoma cruzi  in honor of Oswaldo Cruz [...] he soon found the parasites in the blood of a cat. He then looked for a girl, later identified as Berenice Soares de Moura, a two-year-old girl whom he had seen in the same hut where that cat had been a few weeks before. He took Berenice's blood samples on 14 April 1909, discovering for the first time the same Trypanosoma parasite in the human blood. He also observed parasitic inclusions in the brain and myocardium, which would explain some of the clinical manifestations in diseased people, and closed the proposed lifecycle of the parasite by suggesting that the armadillo could be its natural reservoir. To complete his work on the pathology of the new disease, Chagas described 27 cases of the acute form of the disease and performed more than 100 autopsies on patients who exhibited the chronic form. [...] Chagas was twice nominated for the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, in 1913 and 1921, but never received any. [...] The reason why the prize was not awarded to Chagas may have been the strong opposition that he faced in Brazil, from some physicians and researchers of that time. They went as far as questioning the existence of Chagas disease [...] He was nominated for the Nobel Prize each time by only a single Brazilian nominator. [...] Analysis of the database of the Nobel Prize archives, with the revelation of the names of nominators, nominees, and prizewinners from 1901 to 1951 [...] The connections of the members of the Nobel Committee with the international scientific community, almost exclusively centered in European and North American scientists, also influenced their choices. The nonrecognition of Carlos Chagas' discoveries by the Nobel Committee appears to be more correctly explained by these factors than by the negative impact of the local opposition. [...] After the death of his mentor in 1917, Chagas accepted Cruz's directorship of the institute

gancho: As epidemias de paralisia infantil surgiram quando as cidades ficaram mais limpas. Com menos contato com o vírus na primeira infância, mais gente se infectava mais velha, quando a paralisia é bem mais comum.
explicacao: Grandes epidemias de pólio eram desconhecidas antes do século XX: surtos localizados de paralisia começaram a aparecer na Europa e nos EUA por volta de 1900. Antes disso, a infecção raramente era vista em bebês com menos de 6 meses, e a maioria dos casos ocorria entre os 6 meses e os 4 anos. Crianças pequenas que pegam pólio costumam ter sintomas leves e, com isso, ficam imunes para sempre. No fim do século XIX e começo do XX, os países ricos melhoraram o saneamento, com esgoto e água limpa. Com mais higiene, bebês e crianças pequenas tinham menos chance de encontrar o vírus e criar imunidade, e o primeiro contato passou a acontecer no fim da infância ou na vida adulta. E a idade pesa: a paralisia aparece em 1 de cada 1.000 crianças infectadas, mas em 1 de cada 75 adultos. Em 1950, nos EUA, o pico de casos paralíticos já tinha passado dos bebês para crianças de 5 a 9 anos, e cerca de um terço dos casos era em maiores de 15 anos. Mas a explicação tem limites: um estudo de 2015, com dados dos EUA de meados do século XX, concluiu que o avanço da pólio nessas décadas se explica melhor pelo baby boom, que multiplicou as crianças suscetíveis, do que pela higiene. Os autores admitem, porém, que a higiene pode ter pesado no surgimento das epidemias, por volta de 1900.

fontes.trecho: Major polio epidemics were unknown before the 20th century; localized paralytic polio epidemics began to appear in Europe and the United States around 1900. [...] Prior to the 20th century, polio infections were rarely seen in infants before 6 months of age, and most cases occurred in children 6 months to 4 years of age. Young children who contract polio generally develop only mild symptoms, but as a result they become permanently immune to the disease.  In developed countries during the late 19th and early 20th centuries, improvements were being made in community sanitation, including improved sewage disposal and clean water supplies. Better hygiene meant that infants and young children had fewer opportunities to encounter and develop immunity to polio. Exposure to poliovirus was therefore delayed until late childhood or adult life, when it was more likely to take the paralytic form. In children, paralysis due to polio occurs in one in 1,000 cases, while in adults, paralysis occurs in one in 75 cases. By 1950, the peak age incidence of paralytic poliomyelitis in the United States had shifted from infants to children aged 5 to 9 years; about one-third of the cases were reported in persons over 15 years of age. [...] In the United States, the 1952 polio epidemic was the worst outbreak in the nation's history, and is credited with heightening parents' fears of the disease and focusing public awareness on the need for a vaccine.  Of the 57,628 cases reported that year, 3,145 died

fontes.titulo: Unraveling the Transmission Ecology of Polio (Martinez-Bakker, King e Rohani, PLoS Biology, 2015)
fontes.trecho: We analyzed an extensive epidemiological dataset, spanning the 1930s to the 1950s and spatially replicated across each state in the United States, to glean insight into the drivers of polio’s historical expansion [...] contrary to the prevailing “disease of development” hypothesis, our analyses demonstrate that polio’s historical expansion was straightforwardly explained by demographic trends rather than improvements in sanitation and hygiene [...] Our analyses show that the historical expansion of polio is straightforwardly explained by the demographic “baby boom” during the postwar period rather than improvements in hygiene. [...] Our results suggest the marked increase in polio incidence from the 1930s to the 1950s was a straightforward consequence of increased birth rates [...] changes in hygiene and sanitation could have contributed to the initial emergence of polio, which occurred from the late 1800s to the early 20th century. [...] Martinez-Bakker M, King AA, Rohani P (2015) Unraveling the Transmission Ecology of Polio.

gancho: No século XVI, uma doença misteriosa matou de 5 a 15 milhões de pessoas no México colonial. Os astecas a chamavam de cocoliztli, "peste". Em 2018, DNA dos dentes de vítimas apontou um suspeito, mas o caso segue aberto.
explicacao: As epidemias de cocoliztli, marcadas por febre alta e sangramentos, devastaram as terras altas do México, e a de 1545 costuma ser chamada de a pior epidemia da história do país. Pelo menos 12 surtos são atribuídos à doença, os maiores em 1545, 1576, 1736 e 1813, e em geral eles vinham até dois anos depois de uma grande seca. Os indígenas foram os mais atingidos, seguidos pelos africanos; os europeus morreram menos. Médicos espanhóis e indígenas não souberam identificá-la, e um médico espanhol que viu o surto de 1576 fazia questão de usar o nome em náuatle. Em 2018, a equipe do bioquímico alemão Johannes Krause extraiu DNA dos dentes de 29 pessoas de um cemitério de Oaxaca, o único ligado com segurança às vítimas do surto de 1545 a 1548. Em dez delas apareceu uma variedade rara de salmonela, a Paratyphi C, que causa uma febre parecida com a tifoide e não estava no solo nem em pessoas de antes do contato com os europeus. A bactéria já existia na Europa: foi achada num cemitério norueguês do século XIII. Mas a geneticista María Ávila-Arcos contesta a conclusão, porque os sintomas não batem bem, e vírus de RNA nem foram investigados. Outra hipótese é uma febre hemorrágica nativa, agravada pela pior seca da região em 500 anos e pelas condições impostas aos indígenas depois da conquista.

fontes.trecho: The Cocoliztli Epidemic or the Great Pestilence was an outbreak of a mysterious illness characterized by high fevers and bleeding which caused 5–15 million deaths in the North American territory of New Spain during the 16th century. The Aztec people called it cocoliztli, Nahuatl for pestilence. It ravaged the Mexican highlands in epidemic proportions [...] Based on the death toll, this outbreak is often referred to as the worst epidemic in the history of Mexico. Subsequent outbreaks continued to baffle both Spanish and native physicians, with little consensus among modern researchers on the pathogenesis. [...] Others believe cocoliztli was caused by an indigenous viral hemorrhagic fever, perhaps exacerbated by the worst droughts to affect that region in 500 years and poor living conditions for Indigenous peoples of Mexico following the Spanish conquest (c. 1519). [...] At least 12 epidemics are attributed to cocoliztli, with the largest occurring in 1545, 1576, 1736, and 1813. [...] Cocoliztli epidemics usually occurred within two years of a major drought. [...] However, the modern consensus is that Indigenous people were most affected by cocoliztli, followed by Africans. Europeans experienced lower mortality rates than other groups. [...] Francisco Hernández de Toledo, a Spanish physician, insisted on using the Nahuatl word when describing the disease to correspondents in the Old World. [...] According to Francisco Hernández de Toledo, a physician who witnessed the outbreak in 1576 [...] In 2018, Johannes Krause, a German biochemist at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Human History, and colleagues discovered new evidence for an Old World culprit. DNA samples from the teeth of 29 sixteenth-century skeletons in the Oaxaca region of Mexico [...] The Contact-era site has the only cemetery to be conclusively linked to victims of the outbreak of 1545–1548. [...] Within ten individuals, they identified Salmonella enterica subsp. enterica serovar Paratyphi C, which causes enteric fevers in humans. This strain of Salmonella is unique to humans and was not found in any soil samples or pre-contact individuals that were used as controls. Enteric fevers, also known as typhoid or paratyphoid [...] The recent discovery of S. Paratyphi C within a 13th-century Norwegian cemetery supports these findings. [...] Evolutionary geneticist, María Ávila-Arcos, has questioned this evidence since S. enterica's symptoms are poorly matched with the disease. Ávila-Arcos, Krause’s team, and authors of earlier historical analyses point out that RNA viruses, among other non-bacterial pathogens, have not been investigated.

gancho: O último caso natural de varíola do mundo foi um cozinheiro de hospital na Somália, em 1977. Segundo ele, tinha evitado a vacina por medo da injeção. Décadas depois, morreu trabalhando como vacinador contra a pólio.
explicacao: Ali Maow Maalin trabalhava como cozinheiro no hospital de Merca, no sul da Somália, e às vezes ajudava uma equipe de vacinação da OMS. Em outubro de 1977, foi como guia no carro que levava duas crianças com varíola, vindas de um acampamento nômade, para o isolamento. Acredita-se que ele tenha se infectado nessa curta viagem. Uma das crianças, Habiba Nur Ali, de seis anos, morreu dois dias depois, a última pessoa a morrer de varíola adquirida naturalmente. Maalin teve febre e foi tratado como se fosse malária; quando surgiram as manchas, acharam que era catapora. Como não queria ser isolado, não se apresentou, até que um colega da enfermagem o denunciou. Ele teve a forma mais branda da doença e se recuperou. As versões sobre a vacina dele divergem: um epidemiologista do CDC disse que ela não pegou, e em 2007 o próprio Maalin contou que não se vacinou por medo, porque a injeção parecia doer. A OMS rastreou 161 contatos, 54.777 pessoas foram vacinadas em duas semanas, e ninguém mais adoeceu. Em 1979, a varíola foi declarada erradicada. Maalin depois foi um dos 10 mil voluntários da campanha que livrou a Somália da pólio em 2008, e contava sua história a pais que recusavam a vacina. Morreu de malária em 2013, durante a vacinação que se seguiu à volta do vírus da pólio ao país.

fontes.trecho: was a Somali hospital cook and health worker from Merca who is the last person known to have been infected with naturally occurring Variola minor smallpox. The disease was diagnosed in October 1977 and Maalin made a full recovery. [...] Smallpox was declared to have been eradicated globally by the World Health Organization (WHO) two years later. Maalin was subsequently involved in the successful poliomyelitis eradication campaign in Somalia, and he died of malaria while carrying out polio vaccinations after the re-emergence of the poliovirus in 2013. [...] He worked as a hospital cook, as well as an occasional vaccinator for a WHO smallpox eradication team. [...] According to CDC epidemiologist Jason Weisfeld, one of the people who led the later containment effort in Merca, Maalin had received the smallpox vaccine but it had failed to take effect, and he had not been protected. Other sources state that he had not been vaccinated. It was later revealed in an interview in 2007, Maalin said that he had not been vaccinated, explaining: "I was scared of being vaccinated then. It looked like the shot hurt." [...] On 12 October 1977, two children with smallpox symptoms were discovered at an encampment [...] Maalin, then aged 23, served as a guide to the party taking them in a closed Land Cruiser from the hospital where he worked either to the home of a surveillance supervisor or directly to the isolation camp. He is believed to have been infected during the journey, which lasted no more than 5–15 minutes. One of the children, a six-year-old girl named Habiba Nur Ali, died two days later. She was the last person to die from naturally acquired smallpox. [...] On 22 October, Maalin fell ill with fever and headache, and received malaria treatment in hospital. After four days a rash appeared. Perhaps working on the assumption that he had been successfully vaccinated against smallpox, Maalin was then believed to have chickenpox and was discharged from hospital. [...] Not wishing to be put into isolation, Maalin failed to report himself. On 30 October, a nurse colleague reported him [...] In August 1977, an outbreak developed in a Somali nomadic group of twenty families [...] A total of 161 contacts were identified [...] A total of 54,777 people were vaccinated in the two weeks following Maalin's isolation. [...] Maalin remains the last case of naturally acquired smallpox in the world. On 26 October 1979, two years after the day when Maalin's rash appeared, WHO declared that smallpox had been eradicated globally. [...] Maalin was among the 10,000 volunteers who participated in the effort to eradicate poliomyelitis from Somalia, which succeeded in 2008. [...] "Now when I meet parents who refuse to give their children the polio vaccine, I tell them my story. [...] V. minor was the rarer of the two strains, and causes a much less severe disease

gancho: Parte dos tatus do sul dos EUA carrega a bactéria da hanseníase e pode passá-la a pessoas. Pelo DNA, eles a pegaram de humanos há no máximo alguns séculos, e a suspeita recai sobre os primeiros europeus nas Américas.
explicacao: A bactéria da hanseníase, Mycobacterium leprae, só se multiplica dentro de células vivas e não pode ser cultivada em meios de laboratório, mas há infecções naturais em alguns primatas, em tatus e em esquilos-vermelhos. No centro-sul dos EUA, de 15% a 20% dos tatus de uma espécie carregam a bactéria. Como a temperatura do corpo deles é baixa, seus tecidos costumam acumular quantidades enormes do micróbio. A análise genética das linhagens dos tatus indica origem humana de no máximo algumas centenas de anos, e por isso se suspeita que os animais a pegaram, por acaso, dos primeiros exploradores europeus. A infecção se manteve entre os tatus e pode voltar a pessoas que manuseiam os bichos ou comem sua carne. Na Grã-Bretanha, descobriu-se em 2016 que os esquilos-vermelhos, uma espécie ameaçada, também carregam a doença. A linhagem achada na ilha de Brownsea equivale a uma que se julgava extinta entre humanos desde a Idade Média, e um crânio anterior à conquista normanda, escavado em Suffolk em 2017, tinha DNA de uma linhagem muito parecida. Há quem sugira que o comércio de peles de esquilo, muito valorizadas na época, tenha alimentado a hanseníase medieval na Europa. Hoje, porém, o risco de transmissão dos esquilos selvagens para pessoas parece baixo: o último caso humano adquirido no Reino Unido foi registrado há mais de 200 anos.

fontes.trecho: M. leprae and M. lepromatosis are obligate intracellular pathogens and cannot grow or be cultured outside of host tissues. [...] Naturally occurring infections have been reported in nonhuman primates (including the African chimpanzee, the sooty mangabey, and the cynomolgus macaque), armadillos, and red squirrels. Multilocus sequence typing of the armadillo M. leprae strains suggests that they were of human origin for at most a few hundred years. Thus, it is suspected that armadillos first acquired the organism incidentally from early European explorers of the Americas. This incidental transmission was sustained in the armadillo population. It may be transmitted back to humans, making leprosy a zoonotic disease (spread between humans and animals). Red squirrels (Sciurus vulgaris), a threatened species in Great Britain, were found to carry leprosy in November 2016. It has been suggested that the trade in red squirrel fur, highly prized in the medieval period and intensively traded, may have been responsible for the leprosy epidemic in medieval Europe. A pre-Norman era skull excavated in Hoxne, Suffolk, in 2017 was found to carry DNA from a strain of M. leprae which closely matched the strain carried by modern red squirrels on Brownsea Island. [...] Humans can acquire a leprosy infection from armadillos by handling them or consuming armadillo meat. [...] The M. leprae strain discovered on Brownsea Island is equated to one thought to have died out in the human population in medieval times. Despite this, and speculation regarding past transmission through trade in squirrel furs, there does not seem to be a high risk of squirrel to human transmission from the wild population. Although leprosy continues to be diagnosed in immigrants to the UK, the last known human case of leprosy arising in the UK was recorded over 200 years ago. [...] Between 15 and 20% of Mexican long-nosed armadillos(Dasypus mexicanus) in the south-central United States carry M. leprae. As a result of their low body temperature, their tissues commonly contain massive numbers of organisms

gancho: Em 1904, a Revolta da Vacina, no Rio, levou o governo a suspender a vacinação obrigatória contra a varíola. Em 1908, a cidade enfrentou uma epidemia da doença que matou quase 6.400 pessoas.
explicacao: No começo do século XX, o Rio de Janeiro, então capital, sofria com febre amarela, peste bubônica e varíola. O médico Oswaldo Cruz, que assumiu a Saúde Pública em 1903, comandou campanhas de saneamento, enquanto o prefeito Pereira Passos fazia uma reforma urbana que derrubou cortiços e provocou uma crise de moradia. Em 31 de outubro de 1904, foi aprovada uma lei que tornava obrigatória a vacinação contra a varíola, apesar de forte campanha contrária. Entre 10 e 16 de novembro, a cidade viveu uma semana de motins. Militares florianistas e positivistas tentaram aproveitar a revolta para dar um golpe de Estado, que fracassou. No bairro da Saúde, um dos maiores focos, verificou-se depois que a dinamite pendurada em volta das trincheiras era feita de pedaços de madeira embrulhados em papel prateado, e o canhão, um cano de iluminação pública montado sobre rodas de carroça. No dia 16, o governo decretou estado de sítio e suspendeu a vacinação obrigatória. A repressão deixou 945 presos na Ilha das Cobras, 30 mortos, 110 feridos e 461 deportados para o Acre, e atingiu sobretudo os mais pobres, cuja participação nem sempre foi comprovada. Quatro anos depois, veio a epidemia de varíola de 1908, com quase 6.400 mortos.

fontes.trecho: A Revolta da Vacina foi um motim popular ocorrido entre 10 e 16 de novembro de 1904 na cidade do Rio de Janeiro, então capital do Brasil. Seu pretexto imediato foi uma lei que determinava a obrigatoriedade da vacinação contra a varíola, mas também é associada a causas mais profundas, como as reformas urbanas que estavam sendo realizadas pelo prefeito Pereira Passos e as campanhas de saneamento lideradas pelo médico Oswaldo Cruz. [...] Um grupo de militares florianistas e positivistas, com o apoio de alguns setores civis, tentou se aproveitar do descontentamento popular para realizar um golpe de Estado na madrugada do dia 14 para o dia 15 de novembro, que, no entanto, foi derrotado. No dia 16 de novembro, foi decretado o estado de sítio e a suspensão da vacinação obrigatória. [...] Os maiores focos de revolta estavam concentrados na Saúde e no Sacramento. [...] O saldo total foi de 945 pessoas presas na Ilha das Cobras, 30 mortos, 110 feridos e 461 deportados para o estado do Acre. [...] ico Oswaldo Cruz, que assumiu a Diretoria Geral de Saúde Pública em 1903, coube a campanha de saneamento da cidade, que visava erradicar a febre amarela, a peste bubônica e a varíola. [...] A lei gerou debates exaltados entre os legisladores e a população e, apesar da forte campanha de oposição, foi aprovada no dia 31 de outubro. [...] A demolição dos velhos casarões, àquela altura já quase todos transformados em pensões e cortiços, provocou uma crise de habitação [...] Verificou-se também que as dinamites e bocas-de-fogo não passavam de um engodo. As primeiras eram, na verdade, peças de madeira envoltas em papel prateado, dependuradas por arames em torno das trincheiras, enquanto a boca-de-fogo não passava de um cano de iluminação pública co [...] As vítimas da repressão que se seguiu foram, em geral, os indivíduos mais pobres, que poderiam ter tomado parte na revolta, embora sua participação nem sempre fosse comprovada. [...] a população do Rio de Janeiro teria de suportar uma epidemia de varíola em 1908, na qual morreram quase 6 400 pessoas.

On 16 November, a state of emergency was decreed and mandatory vaccination was suspended. [...] the population of Rio de Janeiro would have to endure a smallpox epidemic in 1908, in which almost 6,400 people died.

gancho: Em 1929, o médico alemão Werner Forssmann enfiou um cateter numa veia do próprio braço e o empurrou até o coração, para provar que isso não matava. Foi punido pela ousadia e, em 1956, dividiu o Nobel.
explicacao: Na época, temia-se que qualquer intrusão no coração fosse fatal. Forssmann, que acabara de passar no exame de Estado de medicina, imaginava que um tubo levado até lá serviria para aplicar remédios, injetar contraste para raios X ou medir a pressão. Ignorando o chefe do departamento, ele convenceu a enfermeira que cuidava do material estéril, Gerda Ditzen, a ajudar. Segundo o relato conhecido, ela só aceitou se o teste fosse feito nela, mas ele a prendeu à mesa de cirurgia, fingiu operá-la e, na verdade, anestesiou o próprio antebraço e introduziu na veia um cateter urinário. Os dois desceram então à sala de raios X, onde ele avançou o tubo por 60 cm e registrou numa chapa a ponta dentro do coração. O chefe, irritado de início, reconheceu o feito ao ver as imagens. Já em Berlim, no hospital Charité, o cirurgião Ferdinand Sauerbruch o dispensou por agir sem sua aprovação. Com a fama de autoexperimentador, Forssmann teve dificuldade de arrumar emprego, largou a cardiologia e virou urologista. Anos depois, os pesquisadores André Cournand e Dickinson Richards leram o artigo dele e transformaram a técnica em ferramenta de diagnóstico de doenças cardíacas. Em 1956, os três dividiram o Nobel de Medicina.

fontes.trecho: shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Medicine (with Andre Frederic Cournand and Dickinson W. Richards) for developing a procedure that allowed cardiac catheterization. In 1929, he put himself under local anesthesia and inserted a catheter into a vein of his arm. [...] passing the State Examination in 1929. [...] He hypothesized that a catheter could be inserted directly into the heart, for such applications as directly delivering drugs, injecting radiopaque dyes, or measuring blood pressure. The fear at the time was that such an intrusion into the heart would be fatal. To prove his point, he decided to try the experiment on himself. [...] He ignored his department chief and persuaded the operating-room nurse in charge of the sterile supplies, Gerda Ditzen, to assist him. She agreed, but only on the promise that he would do it on her rather than on himself. However, Forssmann tricked her by restraining her to the operating table and pretending to locally anaesthetise and cut her arm whilst actually doing it on himself. He anesthetized his own lower arm in the cubital region and inserted a urinary catheter into his antecubital vein [...] They walked some distance to the X-ray department on the floor below where under the guidance of a fluoroscope he advanced the catheter the full 60 cm into his right ventricular cavity. This was then recorded on X-ray film showing the catheter lying in his right atrium. The head clinician at Eberswalde, although initially very annoyed, recognized Werner's discovery when shown the X-rays [...] An unpaid position was created for Forssmann at the Berliner Charité Hospital, working under Ferdinand Sauerbruch, although once Sauerbruch saw his paper, he was dismissed for continuing without his approval. [...] Finding it difficult to get a job with his reputation, he quit cardiology and took up urology. [...] During the time of his imprisonment, his paper was read by André Frédéric Cournand and Dickinson W. Richards. They developed ways of applying his technique to heart disease diagnosis and research. [...] In 1956, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to Cournand, Richards, and Forßmann.

gancho: Para provar que a pelagra não era contagiosa, o médico Joseph Goldberger injetou sangue de doentes em si mesmo, na esposa e em outros voluntários, em 1916. Ninguém pegou a doença: a causa estava na dieta.
explicacao: A pelagra ataca a pele e, só na Carolina do Sul, somava 30 mil casos em 1912. A maioria dos médicos a considerava infecciosa, embalados pelo sucesso recente da teoria dos germes. Goldberger, do serviço de saúde pública dos EUA, notou duas coisas: os funcionários de hospital que lidavam com os doentes não adoeciam, e os casos se concentravam entre os sulistas pobres, que comiam muito alimento derivado do milho. Em dois orfanatos, trocou a comida por uma dieta com carne fresca, verduras, leite e ovos, e os casos novos sumiram. Numa fazenda-prisão do Mississippi sem nenhum caso de pelagra, 11 presos voluntários comeram uma dieta à base de milho em troca de perdão; após seis meses, cinco tinham a doença. A ideia, mesmo assim, encontrou resistência, inclusive de líderes do Sul que não aceitavam ligar a epidemia à pobreza. Daí vieram as chamadas "festas da sujeira": 16 voluntários receberam injeções de sangue de doentes e tiveram diarreia e náusea, mas não pelagra. A peça que faltava apareceu em 1937: a doença vem da falta de niacina, uma vitamina B. Os povos indígenas que domesticaram o milho o preparavam com uma solução alcalina, como a cal, na chamada nixtamalização, que torna a niacina aproveitável. Quando o milho se espalhou pelo mundo sem esse preparo, a pelagra se tornou comum.

fontes.trecho: By 1912, South Carolina alone had 30,000 cases [...] Pellagra was a painful skin disease commonly found in tropical regions. [...] Goldberger's theory that pellagra was associated with diet contradicted the most widely accepted medical opinion that pellagra was an infectious disease. The germ theory of disease had recently become popular [...] which he came to believe through his observation that hospital staff who worked closely with pellagra patients did not fall sick themselves. Furthermore, pellagra cases were overwhelmingly poor Southerners, especially African Americans and sharecroppers. This was a group that often ate filling and starchy but nutrient-poor foods, especially those derived from corn. [...] he investigated two orphanages that were experiencing rampant pellagra. [...] he switched them to a more varied diet that included fresh meat, vegetables, milk, and eggs. After several weeks, there were no new cases [...] He chose this prison in particular because it previously had no cases of pellagra. After negotiation, Earl accepted Goldberger's request in return for pardons for the prisoners [...] Goldberger experimented on 11 healthy volunteers from the Rankin State Prison Farm for this 9-month study. The subjects were put on a strict and heavily monitored corn-based diet lacking meat, milk, and vegetables. [...] After six months, five of the eleven patients contracted pellagra [...] opposition also came from Southern leaders who resented a Northerner claiming that the pellagra outbreak was a product of the region's widespread poverty. [...] He conducted one final experiment, referred to as "filth parties", to silence the critics. In 1916, he injected 16 volunteers—including himself, his wife, and his assistant—with pellagric blood over 7 trials. Afterwards they experienced diarrhea and nausea but did not contract the disease. [...] It was not until 1937 that Conrad Elvehjem discovered that pellagra is caused by a dietary lack of the B vitamin niacin

Native American cultivators who first domesticated corn (maize) prepared it by nixtamalization, in which the grain is treated with a solution of alkali such as lime. Nixtamalization makes the niacin nutritionally available and prevents pellagra. When maize was cultivated worldwide, and eaten as a staple without nixtamalization, pellagra became common.

gancho: Na Polônia ocupada pelos nazistas, intelectuais se protegeram alimentando piolhos com o próprio sangue, para a vacina de Rudolf Weigl contra o tifo. Um desses "alimentadores" foi o matemático Stefan Banach.
explicacao: Em 1909, o francês Charles Nicolle mostrou que os piolhos espalham a bactéria do tifo epidêmico. Em Lwów, o biólogo Rudolf Weigl criou uma vacina feita dos próprios insetos: piolhos eram infectados e depois tinham o intestino extraído e moído numa pasta. Para crescer, eles precisavam se alimentar de sangue, quanto mais humano melhor, e por volta de 1933 Weigl passou a usar pessoas. Os piolhos ficavam em caixinhas de madeira com fundo de tela, e cada alimentador apoiava na perna de 7 a 11 caixas por sessão, cada uma com 400 a 800 larvas. O risco era pegar tifo, e o próprio Weigl adoeceu, mas os voluntários eram vacinados antes e, segundo os registros, nenhum morreu. Quando os alemães tomaram a cidade, em 1941, mantiveram o instituto aberto porque queriam a vacina para os soldados. Weigl usou isso para contratar intelectuais poloneses, ameaçados depois que os nazistas prenderam professores em Cracóvia. Os alimentadores recebiam comida extra, podiam circular pela cidade e estavam protegidos do envio a campos de trabalho escravo e de concentração. Entre eles estavam Banach, o também matemático Władysław Orlicz e o poeta Zbigniew Herbert. Doses da vacina chegaram contrabandeadas aos guetos de Lwów e de Varsóvia. Em 2003, Weigl foi reconhecido em Israel como Justo entre as Nações.

fontes.trecho: Louse-feeders were human sources of blood for lice infected with typhus, which were then used to research possible vaccines against the disease. [...] Weigl and his wife Zofia Weigl were some of the earliest lice feeders. During the Nazi occupation of the city, louse-feeding became the primary means of support and protection for many of the city's Polish intellectuals, including the mathematicians Stefan Banach and Władysław Orlicz and the poet Zbigniew Herbert. While the profession carried a significant risk of infection, louse-feeders were given additional food rations, were protected from being shipped to slave labour camps and German concentration camps, and were permitted to move around the occupied city. [...] French bacteriologist Charles Nicolle showed in 1909 that lice (Pediculus humanus corporis) were the primary means by which the typhus bacteria  (Rickettsia prowazekii) were spread. [...] by 1933, Weigl began using human volunteers as feeders. [...] Weigl protected the donors by vaccinating them beforehand, and although some of them (including Weigl himself) developed the disease, none died. [...] The feeding was done through the use of specially-constructed small wooden boxes [...] the underside consisted of a screen made of a fabric sieve [...] A typical box contained 400 to 800 lice larvae which would mature as the feeding took place. [...] Usually, an individual feeder would accommodate from 7 to 11 boxes (of 400 to 800 lice each) on his or her leg, per feeding session. [...] In June 1941, after the Nazi attack on the Soviet Union, Lwów was taken over by the Germans. [...] was kept open because, much like the Soviets before them, the Germans were interested in the applications of the typhus vaccine among their front line soldiers. [...] In light of the Sonderaktion Krakau, a German operation in which many distinguished professors from Jagiellonian University in Kraków were arrested and sent to German concentration camps, the danger that a similar fate would befall Lwów intellectuals was very real. As a result, in July 1941, Weigl began hiring prominent Polish intellectuals of the city for his institute

developed a technique to produce a typhus vaccine by growing infected lice and crushing them into a vaccine paste. [...] Extracting the lice's midguts and grinding them into a paste (which was the vaccine). Growing lice meant feeding them blood, the more human the better. [...] His vaccines were smuggled into ghettos in Lwów and Warsaw, various concentration camps, and even certain Gestapo prisons. [...] In 2003, he was honored as Righteous Among the Nations. This award was given by Israel

gancho: Em 1799, um médico inglês tratou reumáticos com imitações de madeira dos "tratores" de metal de Elisha Perkins, vendidos como cura para dores. Quatro dos cinco pacientes disseram que a dor aliviou.
explicacao: Os tratores de Perkins, patenteados nos EUA em 1796, eram duas hastes de metal de cerca de 3 polegadas com ponta. Ele dizia que eram feitos de ligas incomuns, embora fossem de aço e latão, e que, passados sobre a parte dolorida por uns 20 minutos, retiravam do corpo um "fluido elétrico nocivo". A Sociedade Médica de Connecticut o expulsou, chamando o método de charlatanice, mas ele convenceu três faculdades de medicina americanas, cirurgiões de um hospital real em Copenhague e até George Washington, que comprou um jogo. O filho de Perkins levou o negócio para Londres. Na Inglaterra, o médico John Haygarth resolveu pôr a ideia à prova: tratou cinco pacientes com reumatismo usando tratores de madeira feitos para parecer os de metal, e quatro relataram alívio. No dia seguinte, usou os de metal, com o mesmo resultado. Haygarth publicou as conclusões num texto sobre a imaginação como causa e como cura dos males do corpo, considerado pioneiro no estudo do que hoje se chama efeito placebo. As vendas continuaram por anos. Perkins, por sua vez, morreu em 1799: tentava curar a febre amarela em Nova York com vinagre e sal, o remédio não funcionou e ele pegou a doença.

fontes.trecho: The device was later the subject of the first placebo research. [...] Consequently, around 1795–96, Perkins invented his "Tractors", for which he took out a 14-year patent on February 19, 1796. The tractors consisted of two 3-inch metal rods with a pointed end [...] Although they were made of steel and brass, Perkins claimed that they were made of unusual metal alloys. Perkins claimed his rods cured inflammation, rheumatism and pain in the head and the face. He applied the points on the aching body part and passed them over the part for about 20 minutes. Perkins claimed they could "draw off the noxious electrical fluid that lay at the root of suffering". The Connecticut Medical Society condemned the tractors as "delusive quackery", and expelled Perkins from membership [...] Perkins nevertheless managed to convince three US medical faculties that his method worked. In Copenhagen, Denmark, twelve surgeons at the royal Frederiks Hospital also began to support the method. Even George Washington bought a set. [...] Benjamin Perkins was a bookseller and introduced the tractors to London. [...] This consisted of vinegar with muriate of soda which he tested in New York City during an outbreak in 1799. The cure had no effect and Perkins contracted the fever and died. After Perkins' death, British physicians began to have doubts about his tractors. In 1799, Dr. John Haygarth conducted a test in which he treated five rheumatic patients with wooden tractors that were made to resemble the metallic ones. Four of them reported that the pain was relieved. The next day the patients were treated with metallic tractors with the same results. Dr. Haygarth reported on his findings in a publication entitled On the Imagination as a Cause & as a Cure of Disorders of the Body. [...] By this time, Perkins had numerous influential supporters and the sale of the tractors continued.

gancho: O estetoscópio nasceu de um constrangimento: em 1816, o médico René Laennec achou impróprio encostar o ouvido no peito de uma jovem paciente, enrolou um maço de papel em tubo e ouviu o coração dela melhor que nunca.
explicacao: Até então, para ouvir o coração e os pulmões, os médicos apoiavam o ouvido direto no peito do paciente. No caso daquela jovem, com sintomas de doença cardíaca, bater no peito ou apalpá-lo ajudava pouco por causa da gordura, e a escuta direta era inadmissível pela idade e pelo sexo dela. Laennec, que também entalhava as próprias flautas de madeira, lembrou que o arranhar de um alfinete numa ponta de uma peça de madeira se ouve com nitidez na outra. O tubo de papel funcionou, e ele fez depois um cilindro oco de madeira de 25 cm. Mais que o objeto, criou um método: acompanhava os doentes do leito à mesa de autópsia e ligava cada som ao que encontrava nos órgãos. Foi assim que passou a identificar melhor doenças como a tuberculose e a classificar ruídos como os estertores, termos que os médicos usam até hoje. Batizou o aparelho de estetoscópio, do grego para "peito" e "exame". Nem todos aderiram: em 1885, um professor de medicina ainda mandava usar os ouvidos, e não o estetoscópio. A mãe de Laennec morrera de tuberculose quando ele tinha cinco anos, e ele morreu da mesma doença em 1826, aos 45 anos.

fontes.trecho: His skill at carving his own wooden flutes led him to invent the stethoscope in 1816 [...] He went into a coma and subsequently died of tuberculosis on 13 August 1826, at age 45. [...] His mother died of tuberculosis when he was five years old [...] consulted by a young woman laboring under general symptoms of diseased heart, and in whose case percussion and the application of the hand were of little avail on account of the great degree of fatness. The other method just mentioned direct auscultation being rendered inadmissible by the age and sex of the patient, I happened to recollect a simple and well-known fact in acoustics, ... the great distinctness with which we hear the scratch of a pin at one end of a piece of wood on applying our ear to the other. Immediately, on this suggestion, I rolled a quire of paper into a kind of cylinder and applied one end of it to the region of the heart and the other to my ear, and was not a little surprised and pleased to find that I could thereby perceive the action of the heart in a manner much more clear and distinct than I had ever been able to do by the immediate application of my ear. [...] He built his first instrument as a 25 cm by 2.5 cm hollow wooden cylinder [...] His clinical work allowed him to follow chest patients from bedside to the autopsy table. He was therefore able to correlate sounds captured by his new instruments with specific pathological changes in the chest [...] Tuberculosis, for example, was one ailment he could more clearly identify using his knowledge of typical and atypical chest sounds. Laennec was the first to classify and discuss the terms rales, rhonchi, crepitance, and egophony – terms that doctors now use on a daily basis [...] He named his instrument the stethoscope, from the Greek words στήθος[stethos] (chest), and σκοπός[skopos] (examination). [...] as late as 1885, a professor of medicine stated, "He that hath ears to hear, let him use his ears and not a stethoscope."

Laennec invented the stethoscope because he was not comfortable placing his ear directly onto a woman's chest in order to listen to her heart. He observed that a rolled piece of paper, placed between the individual's chest and his ear, could amplify heart sounds without requiring physical contact.

gancho: Por séculos, boticários europeus venderam múmias egípcias como remédio. Na origem, houve um erro de tradução: "mumia" era o nome de um betume medicinal persa, não de corpos embalsamados.
explicacao: Na medicina persa e árabe, mūmiyā era uma espécie de betume preto, usado em cortes, contusões e fraturas e também tomado contra úlceras de estômago e tuberculose. O melhor vinha de uma montanha em Darabgerd, na Pérsia, e era raro e caro; por volta do século XII, o betume importado ficou escasso na Europa. Os egípcios antigos também usavam betume para embalsamar, e a semelhança entre essas substâncias escuras confundiu os tradutores medievais. Na versão latina de um texto do médico árabe Serapião, o Jovem, a mumia virou o material das sepulturas misturado ao líquido do corpo humano. A partir do século XII, passou-se a raspar uma resina preta das múmias, depois a vender múmias inteiras, num comércio lucrativo entre o Egito e a Europa. Quando o Egito proibiu a exportação, no século XVI, boticários europeus passaram a falsificar o produto com cadáveres frescos, embalsamados e secos. Ainda no século XVI, o naturalista francês Pierre Belon concluiu que os árabes falavam de betume e que os tradutores tinham entendido errado. Mesmo assim, no século XVII o físico Robert Boyle elogiava a mumia como remédio para quedas e hematomas. As dúvidas cresceram no século XVIII, mas ainda houve venda ocasional no começo do século XX. O engano também deixou marca na língua: em inglês, mummy designou primeiro o remédio, por volta de 1400, e só em 1615 aparece registrado como corpo embalsamado.

fontes.trecho: Mummia, mumia, or originally mummy was any of several different preparations in the history of medicine, from "mineral pitch" to "powdered human mummies". [...] Beginning around the 12th century when supplies of imported natural bitumen ran short, mummia was misinterpreted as "mummy", and the word's meaning expanded to "a black resinous exudate scraped out from embalmed Egyptian mummies". This began a period of lucrative trade between Egypt and Europe, and suppliers substituted rare mummia exudate with entire mummies, either embalmed or desiccated. After Egypt banned the shipment of mummia in the 16th century, unscrupulous European apothecaries began to sell fraudulent mummia prepared by embalming and desiccating fresh corpses. By the 18th century, doubts about mummia's medical value had grown and its use became rarer, though it was still occasionally sold into the early 20th century. [...] Mummy was first recorded meaning "a medicinal preparation of the substance of mummies; hence, an unctuous liquid or gum used medicinally" (c. 1400) [...] The third mummy meaning was "the body of a human being or animal embalmed (according to the ancient Egyptian or some analogous method) as a preparation for burial" (1615) [...] The usage of mumiya as medicine began with the famous Persian mumiya black pissasphalt remedy for wounds and fractures, which was confused with similarly appearing black bituminous materials used in Egyptian mummification. This was misinterpreted by Medieval Latin translators to mean whole mummies. [...] Medieval Persian physicians used bitumen/asphalt both as a salve for cuts, bruises, and bone fractures, and as an internal medicine for stomach ulcers and tuberculosis. They achieved the best results with a black pissasphalt that seeped from a mountain in Darabgerd, Persia. [...] considered to be an equivalent substitute for the scarce and expensive Persian mumiya. [...] The Arab physician Serapion the Younger (fl. 12th century) wrote about bituminous mumia and its many uses, but the Latin translation of Simon Geneunsis (d. 1303) said, "Mumia, this is the mumia of the sepulchers with aloes and myrrh mixed with the liquid (humiditate) of the human body". [...] The French naturalist Pierre Belon (1517–1564) concluded that the Arab physicians, from whom the western writers derived their knowledge of mumia, had actually referred to the pissasphalt of Dioscorides, which had been misconstrued by the translators. [...] The physicist Robert Boyle (1627–1691) praised it as "one of the useful medicines commended and given by our physicians for falls and bruises

gancho: Em 1960, recém-chegada à agência de remédios dos EUA, a médica Frances Kelsey se recusou a liberar a talidomida, já aprovada em mais de 20 países. No ano seguinte, a droga foi ligada a graves malformações em bebês.
explicacao: A talidomida era vendida como calmante e analgésico, e o pedido da fabricante Richardson-Merrell previa receitá-la a grávidas contra o enjoo matinal. Kelsey, uma das sete médicas e médicos que revisavam remédios em tempo integral na FDA, achou que os depoimentos enviados pela empresa não tinham método científico. A agência só podia segurar uma aprovação por 60 dias de cada vez, então ela pedia novos dados a cada 60 dias, e fez isso por mais de um ano. Uma carta publicada no British Medical Journal ligando a droga a sintomas neurológicos reforçou a suspeita e a fez lembrar de seus estudos sobre como surgem as malformações. Ela exigiu então testes em animais que mostrassem que o feto não seria prejudicado. O representante da empresa se irritou e tentou acelerar o processo, mas os chefes dela a apoiaram. Em novembro de 1961, nascimentos de bebês com malformações na Europa foram ligados à talidomida tomada pelas mães na gravidez. Nos EUA, a empresa já tinha distribuído comprimidos "experimentais" a dezenas de milhares de pacientes, com 17 casos de malformação confirmados. Em 1962, Kelsey foi condecorada pelo presidente John F. Kennedy, e o caso ajudou a aprovar uma lei que passou a exigir que a eficácia de um remédio fosse comprovada antes da venda.

fontes.trecho: As a reviewer, she refused to authorize thalidomide for market because she had concerns about the lack of evidence regarding the drug's safety. Her concerns proved to be justified when it was shown that thalidomide caused serious birth defects. [...] Working with Geiling led to her interest in teratogens, drugs that cause birth defects. She learned about the mechanism by which birth defects occur. [...] In 1960, Kelsey was hired by the FDA in Washington, D.C. At that time, she "was one of only seven full-time and four young part-time physicians reviewing drugs" for the FDA. [...] One of her first assignments at the FDA was to review an application by Richardson-Merrell for the drug thalidomide (under the tradename Kevadon) as a tranquilizer and painkiller with specific indications to prescribe the drug to pregnant women for morning sickness. Although it had been previously approved in Canada and more than 20 European and African countries, she withheld approval for the drug and requested to see clinical trial information. At the time, the FDA could only withhold approval for 60 days at a time, so she continually requested further information from the company every 60 days for over a year. Her initial reason for doing this was that the testimonials supplied by Richardson-Merrell contained no scientific methodology [...] In December 1960, Leslie Florence published a letter in the British Medical Journal connecting thalidomide to neurological symptoms. [...] The unexpected neurological effects caused her to recall her earlier work on the mechanism of birth defects, so she also requested animal studies to demonstrate that the drug would not be harmful to the fetus. [...] Kelsey's continual requests for more information incurred the ire of her contact at Richardson-Merrell, who insisted on speeding up the approval process and attempted to escalate the application, but Kelsey's superiors at the FDA stood by her. Kelsey's insistence that the drug should be fully tested prior to approval was vindicated in November 1961 when the births of deformed infants in Europe were linked to thalidomide ingestion by their mothers during pregnancy. [...] In March 1962, after distributing "experimental" tablets to tens of thousands of patients without approval (with 17 malformed births confirmed and dozens more suspected), Richardson-Merrell at last withdrew their FDA application. [...] The amendments, for the first time, also recognized that "effectiveness [should be] required to be established prior to marketing." [...] Kelsey was awarded the President's Award for Distinguished Federal Civilian Service by John F. Kennedy on August 7, 1962

gancho: Campeão amador de golfe dos EUA, o milionário Eben Byers tomou cerca de 1.400 frascos de um tônico de água com rádio. Perdeu quase toda a mandíbula, morreu em 1932 e foi enterrado num caixão forrado de chumbo.
explicacao: Em 1927, Byers machucou o braço ao cair de um beliche de trem, e um médico lhe sugeriu o Radithor contra a dor. O produto, rádio dissolvido em água, era feito por William Bailey, que abandonara Harvard, se apresentava falsamente como médico e pagava aos médicos uma comissão por dose receitada. Era anunciado como "cura para os mortos-vivos" e prometia até curar a impotência. Byers chegou a tomar várias doses por dia, dizendo que se sentia revigorado, até parar em 1930, quando o efeito sumiu. Emagreceu, passou a ter dores de cabeça e os dentes começaram a cair. Em 1931, doente demais para viajar e depor sobre o caso, recebeu em casa um advogado do governo, que relatou que quase toda a mandíbula superior e a maior parte da inferior tinham sido removidas e que se abriam buracos no crânio dele. O mecanismo: engolido, o rádio se acumula nos ossos, e ali sua radiação alfa, que a pele barraria se viesse de fora, causa um estrago intenso nas células. A morte de Byers teve muita repercussão, ajudou a derrubar a moda dos remédios radioativos e reforçou os poderes da FDA. Quando o corpo foi exumado para estudo, em 1965, ainda era radioativo.
