Em 1928, Selmar Aschheim e Bernhard Zondek mostraram que a urina de mulheres no começo da gravidez, injetada em camundongos fêmeas imaturos, fazia os ovários crescerem e amadurecerem folículos. Em 1931, Maurice Friedman e Maxwell Lapham, da Universidade da Pensilvânia, trocaram o camundongo por uma coelha. Alguns dias depois da injeção, o animal era dissecado e o tamanho dos ovários era examinado. Esse "teste do coelho" se espalhou, e a expressão, registrada a partir de 1949, gerou o eufemismo "the rabbit died" para um resultado positivo. Muita gente supunha que a coelha morria apenas quando a mulher estava grávida, mas todas morriam, já que o exame dependia de abrir o animal. A precisão desses testes com roedores e coelhos foi estimada entre 82,5% e 99,5%, e eles foram usados em grande escala dos anos 1930 até o começo dos anos 1960. Uma alternativa posterior, com rãs africanas, dava o resultado sem precisar matar o animal.

fontes.trecho: The rabbit test, or Friedman test, was an early pregnancy test that required killing and dissecting a rabbit to obtain the results. The test was developed in 1931 by Maurice Friedman and Maxwell Edward Lapham at the University of Pennsylvania. [...] The hormone human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) is produced during pregnancy and can be found in a pregnant woman's urine and blood [...] An earlier test, known as the AZ test, was developed by Selmar Aschheim and Bernhard Zondek. When urine from a woman in the early months of pregnancy was injected into immature female mice, their ovaries would enlarge and show follicular maturation. [...] Friedman and Lapham's test was essentially identical, but replaced the mouse with a rabbit. A few days after the injection, the animal would be dissected and the size of her ovaries examined. [...] The term "rabbit test" was first recorded in 1949, and was the origin of a common euphemism, "the rabbit died", for a positive pregnancy test. The phrase was, in fact, based on a common misconception about the test. While many people assumed that the injected rabbit would die only if the woman was pregnant, in fact all rabbits used for the test died, as they had to be dissected in order to examine the ovaries. A later alternative to the rabbit test, known as the Hogben test, used the African clawed frog, and yielded results without the need to cut the animal open.
Selmar Aschheim and Bernhard Zondek introduced testing based on the presence of human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) in 1928.

fontes.titulo: From Cereal Grains to Immunochemistry: What Role Have Antibodies Played in the History of the Home Pregnancy Test (Antibodies, 2023, via Europe PMC)
fontes.trecho: Interestingly, the accuracy of the A–Z test and the Friedman test was estimated to be around 82.5–99.5%. Both of these tests were used on a massive scale from the 1930s until the early 1960s

gancho: Por mais de um século, uma família de cirurgiões guardou em segredo o fórceps, que ajudava a tirar bebês vivos em partos difíceis. Os instrumentos dela só foram achados em 1813, no sótão de uma casa inglesa.
explicacao: Os Chamberlen eram huguenotes da Normandia que fugiram da violência religiosa na França e se mudaram para a Inglaterra em 1569. O inventor do fórceps obstétrico foi provavelmente Peter Chamberlen, o velho, que atendia partos da rainha Henriqueta Maria, mulher de Carlos I. O sucesso da família junto à realeza e à alta nobreza vinha em parte desse instrumento "secreto", que permitia o nascimento de uma criança viva em casos difíceis. A ideia era separar os dois braços de uma pinça e colocá-los no canal de parto um depois do outro, algo impossível com as pinças comuns. Em 1670, Hugh Chamberlen, sobrinho-neto do inventor, tentou vender o instrumento em Paris, mas a demonstração diante de François Mauriceau, responsável pela maternidade do Hôtel-Dieu, terminou com a morte da mãe e do bebê. Hugh teria vendido o segredo a obstetras holandeses no início do século XVIII, mas há dúvidas sobre o que eles de fato receberam. Modelos derivados só apareceram aos poucos na Inglaterra e na Escócia em 1735. Em 1813, ferramentas de parto de Peter Chamberlen foram descobertas no sótão de Woodham Mortimer Hall, perto de Maldon, junto com luvas, moedas antigas e bugigangas.

fontes.trecho: The obstetric forceps were introduced into the European practice by the eldest son of the Chamberlen family of surgeons. The Chamberlens were French Huguenots from Normandy who worked in Paris before they migrated to England in 1569 to escape the religious violence in France. [...] The inventor was probably the eldest Peter Chamberlen the elder, who became obstetrician-surgeon of Queen Henriette, wife of King Charles I of England [...] The success of this dynasty of obstetricians with the royal family and high nobles was related in part to the use of this "secret" instrument allowing delivery of a live child in difficult cases. In fact, the instrument was kept secret for 150 years by the Chamberlen family. Hugh Chamberlen the elder, grandnephew of Peter the eldest, tried to sell the instrument in Paris in 1670, but the demonstration he performed in front of François Mauriceau, responsible for Paris Hotel-Dieu maternity, was a failure which resulted in the death of mother and child. The secret may have been sold by Hugh Chamberlen to Dutch obstetricians at the start of the 18th century in Amsterdam, but there are doubts about the authenticity of what was actually provided to buyers. [...] Models derived from the Chamberlen instrument finally appeared gradually in England and Scotland in 1735. [...] In 1813, Peter Chamberlen's midwifery tools were discovered at Woodham Mortimer Hall near Maldon (UK) in the attic of the house. The instruments were found along with gloves, old coins and trinkets. [...] The Chamberlen family's forceps were based on the idea of separating the two branches of "sugar clamp" (as those used to remove "stones" from bladder), which were put in place one after another in the birth canal. This was not possible with conventional tweezers previously tested.
Chamberlen became surgeon to Queen Anne of Denmark, wife of James I and accoucheur to Queen Henrietta Maria, Charles I's queen.

gancho: Nos EUA do início do século XX, bebês prematuros em incubadoras eram atração de parque de diversões: o público pagava 25 centavos para vê-los. As entradas bancavam o tratamento, de graça para os pais.
explicacao: O responsável era Martin Couney, nascido Michael Cohen em 1869, na Prússia. Ele se apresentava como médico formado na Europa, mas não há registro de que tenha estudado medicina. Depois de exibir incubadoras em feiras europeias a partir de 1896, levou a atração aos Estados Unidos. Ficou famoso pelo "Infantorium" de Coney Island, em Nova York, e manteve outro em Atlantic City de 1905 a 1943. Na época, muitos achavam que os prematuros eram fracos demais para chegar à vida adulta, e o movimento eugenista, então no auge, criticava os esforços para salvá-los; muitos eram deixados para morrer. Cada incubadora tinha cerca de 1,5 m de altura, paredes de aço e frente de vidro; água quente corria em canos sob o bebê, um termostato regulava a temperatura e o ar passava por filtros de lã. O tratamento era caro, mas Couney não cobrava dos pais: as entradas pagavam tudo, inclusive bons salários às enfermeiras. Revistas médicas condenavam o espetáculo, e quando uma feira fechava ele tentava doar as incubadoras a hospitais, que nunca aceitavam. Quando morreu, em 1950, as incubadoras já estavam nos hospitais públicos. Atribui-se aos seus Infantoriums a sobrevivência de mais de 6.500 prematuros.

fontes.trecho: Martin Arthur Couney (born Michael Cohen, 1869 – March 1, 1950) [...] was best known in medical circles and public view for his amusement park sideshow, "The Infantorium", in which visitors paid 25 cents to view prematurely born babies displayed in incubators. [...] Couney is best-known for his Infantorium at Coney Island, New York. During Couney's active years at fairgrounds across America, it was widely believed that premature babies were "weaklings", who were unfit to survive into adulthood. Couney was one of the first advocates for premature babies, and his Infantoriums have become widely accredited with saving the lives of over 6,500 premature babies. [...] in 1869 in the town of Krotoszyn, which was then part of German Prussia and is now Poland. [...] Couney stated he had studied in Leipzig and Berlin and that his medical licence was European [...] However, there is no record of Couney ever studying medicine in any European institution. [...] In 1896, Couney entered his first exhibition [...] Each incubator at Couney's Infantorium measured around 1.5m high, with steel walls, framework and a glass front. In order to fill the incubators with warm air, water boilers fed warm water into pipes that ran underneath where the babies rested, and thermostats were placed inside the incubators to maintain and regulate temperatures. [...] the air fed into the pipes was first filtered through wool suspended in antiseptic, then again through dry wool. [...] he also established a similar exhibit in Atlantic City which ran for 38 years, from 1905 to 1943. [...] In 1903, the average cost for the care of one infant at Couney's facility was $15 [...] Couney did not charge the parents of his patients for their care. Couney made up the costs of caring for the infants through the entrance fees during the exhibitions. The entrance fees covered not only the care of the infants, but also allowed Couney to pay his nurses a good wage [...] medical journals at the time condemned the shows as risky and dangerous for the premature infants. [...] Throughout Couney's career, whenever a midway or fairground closed, Couney attempted to donate his incubators to local hospitals, though his donations were never accepted. By the year of Couney's death in March 1950, incubators had been integrated into public hospitals. [...] The eugenics movement was reaching its peak at the beginning of the 20th century [...] articles in medical journals questioned efforts to save premature infants [...] premature babies were often left to die without medical intervention.

gancho: Com um minuto de vida, o bebê já recebe uma nota de 0 a 10. A escala foi criada em 1952 por Virginia Apgar, uma anestesista que o chefe da cirurgia tinha desencorajado de ser cirurgiã.
explicacao: Virginia Apgar se formou em 1933 na faculdade de medicina da Universidade Columbia, uma das nove mulheres numa turma de 90, e fez residência em cirurgia. Allen Whipple, chefe da cirurgia, a desencorajou de seguir carreira, dizendo ter visto muitas mulheres tentarem e fracassarem, e a incentivou a ir para a anestesia, área que precisava avançar. Ela foi a primeira mulher a chefiar uma divisão de especialidade no hospital Columbia-Presbyterian e, em 1949, a primeira mulher professora titular da faculdade. Apgar notou que, entre os anos 1930 e 1950, a mortalidade infantil nos EUA caía, mas as mortes nas primeiras 24 horas de vida não. Conta-se que, quando um residente perguntou o que avaliar num recém-nascido, ela anotou num guardanapo cinco itens: cor da pele, pulso, reação a estímulos, tônus muscular e respiração, cada um valendo de 0 a 2. Mais tarde, as letras do sobrenome dela viraram um acrônimo em inglês para os cinco critérios. Apgar registrou que bebês com nota de 0 a 2 tinham mortalidade de 14%; de 3 a 7, de 1,1%; e de 8 a 10, de 0,13%. Hoje a avaliação é feita no primeiro e no quinto minuto de vida. A nota 10 é rara, porque é comum o bebê ter um tom azulado passageiro.

fontes.trecho: In 1952, she developed the 10-point Apgar score to assist physicians and nurses in assessing the status of newborns. [...] In 1933, she graduated fourth in her class from Columbia University College of Physicians and Surgeons (P&S) and completed a residency in surgery at P&S in 1937. Apgar was one of nine women in her class of 90 medical students. She was discouraged by Allen Whipple, the chairman of surgery at Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center, from continuing her career as a surgeon because he had seen many women attempt to be successful surgeons and ultimately fail. He instead encouraged her to practice anesthesiology because he felt that advancements in anesthesia were needed to further advance surgery [...] Apgar was the first woman to head a specialty division at Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center [...] In 1949, Apgar became the first woman to become a full professor at P&S [...] Between the 1930s and the 1950s, the United States infant mortality rate decreased, but the number of infant deaths within the first 24 hours after birth remained constant. [...] The Apgar score was born when Apgar was asked by an obstetrical resident what his newborn examination should cover, she wrote on a napkin five categories in which a newborn child should be evaluated, including appearance, pulse, grimace (reflexes to touch), activity, and respiration. [...] Each section of the five category scale is worth a maximum of two points. Apgar noted newborns that received cumulative scores of 0-2 had an infant death rate of 14%, infants who scored 3-7 had a death rate of 1.1%, and the infants who received scores of 8-10 had a very low mortality rate of 0.13%

The Apgar score is a quick way for health professionals to evaluate the health of all newborns at one and five minutes after birth [...] For each criterion, newborns can receive a score from 0 to 2. The list of criteria is a backronym of Apgar's surname. [...] A score of 10 is uncommon due to the prevalence of transient cyanosis

gancho: O ultrassom da gravidez nasceu numa fábrica de caldeiras. Em 1955, um professor de obstetrícia levou tumores e cistos para testar num aparelho que procurava rachaduras em soldas. A fábrica deu um bife para comparar.
explicacao: Ian Donald serviu como médico na força aérea britânica na Segunda Guerra, onde conheceu técnicas de radar e sonar. Em 1954 virou professor de obstetrícia e ginecologia na Universidade de Glasgow. O marido de uma paciente dirigia a Babcock & Wilcox, fabricante de caldeiras que usava ultrassom para achar trincas e falhas em soldas, e o convidou para conhecer a fábrica de Renfrew. Em 21 de julho de 1955, Donald chegou com miomas e um grande cisto de ovário retirados de pacientes; a empresa forneceu um bife enorme como controle. Mesmo com o aparelho primitivo, cisto e tumor sólido devolviam ecos bem diferentes. Donald conseguiu um detector de falhas industrial e, com o engenheiro Tom Brown, montou um aparelho em cima de uma velha cama de hospital, com correntes e engrenagens de brinquedo Meccano. Um dos primeiros sucessos foi uma mulher dada como vítima de câncer de estômago terminal: o exame sugeriu um cisto, e a cirurgia retirou um cisto benigno que ocupava o abdome inteiro. Em 1958, Donald, John MacVicar e Brown publicaram na revista The Lancet um artigo que trazia a primeira imagem de ultrassom de um feto já publicada.

fontes.trecho: At the start of World War II, Donald was drafted into the Royal Air Force as a medical officer, where he developed an interest in radar and sonar. [...] In September 1954, Donald was promoted to Regius Professor of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the University of Glasgow. [...] wrote an article in The Lancet: "Investigation of Abdominal Masses by Pulsed Ultrasound". The article contained the first published ultrasound image of a fetus. The development of Donald's interest in ultrasound started when one of his patients introduced her husband to him. The patient's husband was the director of the boiler fabrication company Babcock and Wilcox, and he offered a tour of the plant to Donald, who accepted. The Renfrew company was a large user of industrial ultrasound that was used to check for crack and flaws in welds. Donald's purpose in making the visit to Renfrew on 21 July 1955 was to determine if the industrial detecting equipment could be used to differentiate types of tissue. He arrived at the plant with a number of fibroids and a large ovarian cyst taken from gynaecology patients. [...] Donald experimented with the tissue samples along with a huge steak the company had provided for a control [...] even with the primitive apparatus of those days clearly showed that a cyst produced echoes only at depth from the near and far walls, whereas a solid tumour progressively attenuated echoes [...] He obtained a Kelvin Hughes Mark lIb supersonic flaw detector [...] invited Donald to use his detector on a woman who was dying from supposed stomach cancer. [...] MacVicar not knowing the background of the case, commented, "It looks like a cyst." [...] To his surprise, he discovered it was a pseudomucinous cyst that filled the whole abdomen and was histologically benign. [...] The machine was built on top an old hospital bed and made extensive use of Meccano chains and sprockets. [...] In a landmark paper on 7 June 1958 published by Donald, McVicar and Brown

gancho: Na gravidez, células do bebê passam para o corpo da mãe e podem ficar lá por décadas. Num estudo, 63% dos cérebros de mulheres examinados após a morte tinham DNA masculino, provavelmente de filhos homens.
explicacao: O fenômeno se chama microquimerismo, nome inspirado na Quimera da mitologia grega: a presença de algumas células vindas de outro indivíduo, geneticamente diferentes. Na forma mais comum em humanos, células do feto atravessam a placenta e formam linhagens dentro da mãe, onde já foram vistas persistindo e se multiplicando por várias décadas. Depois do parto, cerca de 50% a 75% das mulheres carregam linhagens de células imunes do feto. O caminho inverso também existe: células da mãe ficam no filho, com frequência mais ou menos pela metade. Em 2012, um estudo do centro Fred Hutchinson, em Seattle, examinou o cérebro de 59 mulheres que morreram entre 32 e 101 anos. Havia DNA masculino em 63% delas, em várias regiões do cérebro, e a mais velha com esse DNA tinha 94 anos. Para os autores, células fetais provavelmente atravessam com frequência a barreira que protege o cérebro. O que essas células fazem ainda não se sabe. Uma hipótese as liga a doenças autoimunes; outra diz que elas vão a tecidos lesionados da mãe e ajudam a repará-los, como células-tronco; e é possível também que sejam apenas passageiras inofensivas.

fontes.trecho: Microchimerism is the presence of a small number of cells in an individual that have originated from another individual and are therefore genetically distinct. [...] The term comes from the prefix "micro" + "chimerism" based on the hybrid Chimera of Greek mythology. [...] In humans (and perhaps in all placental mammals), the most common form is fetomaternal microchimerism (also known as fetal cell microchimerism or fetal chimerism) whereby cells from a fetus pass through the placenta and establish cell lineages within the mother. Fetal cells have been documented to persist and multiply in the mother for several decades. [...] The potential health consequences of these cells are unknown. One hypothesis is that these fetal cells might trigger a graft-versus-host reaction leading to autoimmune disease. [...] Another hypothesis is that fetal cells come to injured or diseased maternal tissue where they act as stem cells and participate in repair. It is also possible that the fetal cells are merely innocent bystanders and have no effect on maternal health. After giving birth, about 50–75% of women carry fetal immune cell lines. Maternal immune cells are also found in the offspring yielding in maternal→fetal microchimerism, though this phenomenon is about half as frequent as the former.

fontes.titulo: Men on the mind: Study finds male DNA in women's brains (Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, 2012)
fontes.trecho: Sept. 26, 2012 – Male DNA is commonly found in the brains of women, most likely derived from prior pregnancy with a male fetus [...] The findings support the likelihood that fetal cells frequently cross the human blood-brain barrier and that microchimerism in the brain is relatively common. [...] For this research, scientists examined brain autopsy specimens from 59 women who had died between the ages of 32 and 101. Male microchimerism was detected in 63 percent of subjects, was distributed in multiple brain regions, and was potentially persistent throughout the human lifespan; the oldest female in whom male fetal DNA was detected in the brain was 94.

gancho: Um gene essencial para a placenta humana veio de um vírus que infectou nossos ancestrais há mais de 25 milhões de anos. Camundongos usam genes com a mesma função, mas capturados de outros vírus.
explicacao: O gene ERVW-1 produz a sincitina-1, uma proteína que faz células se fundirem. Ele é o que restou de uma infecção antiga por um retrovírus que se instalou nas células reprodutivas de primatas e passou a ser herdado; a integração provavelmente ocorreu há mais de 25 milhões de anos. Por isso o gene existe em humanos, nos grandes macacos e nos macacos do Velho Mundo, mas não nos do Novo Mundo. Nos vírus, as proteínas desse tipo, do envelope, ajudam o vírus a entrar na célula. Na placenta, a sincitina funde células do trofoblasto e forma o sinciciotrofoblasto, uma camada que é uma única célula com muitos núcleos. É ela que fica entre o feto e o sangue da mãe: permite a troca de nutrientes e resíduos e barra a passagem de células imunes da mãe. Os outros genes do vírus original acumularam mutações e deixaram de funcionar; só o do envelope seguiu ativo. Temos ainda a sincitina-2, de outra família de vírus, presente tanto nos macacos do Velho quanto nos do Novo Mundo (mas ausente nos prossímios) e com idade estimada em 45 milhões de anos. Os camundongos têm as sincitinas A e B, sem parentesco com as humanas, que entraram na linhagem deles há mais de 20 milhões de anos. Por isso há a hipótese de que a captura desses genes virais tenha ajudado no próprio surgimento dos mamíferos placentários.

fontes.trecho: Syncytin-1 also known as enverin is a protein found in humans and other primates that is encoded by the ERVW-1 gene (endogenous retrovirus group W envelope member 1). Syncytin-1 is a cell-cell fusion protein whose function is best characterized in placental development. [...] The gene encoding this protein is an endogenous retroviral element that is the remnant of an ancient retroviral infection endogenized into the primate germ line. In the case of syncytin-1 (which is found in humans, apes, and Old World but not New World monkeys), this integration likely occurred more than 25 million years ago. [...] both of which contain nonsense mutations rendering them non-coding. [...] Syncytin-1 mediated trophoblast fusion is essential for normal placental development. [...] the syncytiotrophoblast is one, fully differentiated, non dividing, fused cell syncytium. [...] The syncytiotrophoblast layer is the interface between the developing fetus and the maternal blood supply [...] The placental barrier enables nutrient and waste exchange, while blocking maternal immune and other cells, particles and molecules from passing into the fetal blood circulation.

It is a member of the HERV-FRD family of endogenous retroviral elements. [...] In both Syncytin-2 and Syncytin-1, in their structures, the env gene is complete and able to encode for fusogenic activity, but their gag and pol genes are disrupted. [...] This gene is conserved among all primates, with an estimated age of 45 million years, and entered the primate genome before Syncytin-1. Specifically, this protein entered the genome before the split between New World and Old-World Monkeys. However, this protein is absent in prosimians. [...] The mouse syncytins are not true orthologues. In mice, they are syncytin-A and syncytin-B, and are unrelated to the human syncytin one and two, and entered the lineage 20 million plus years ago. [...] it is hypothesized that the capture of these retroviral envelope genes, could have potentially played as a factor in the emergence of placental mammals altogether.

Retroviral fusogenic env proteins, which play a role in the entry of the virion into the host cell, have had an important impact on the development of the mammalian placenta. In mammals, intact env proteins called syncytins are responsible for the formation and function of syncytiotrophoblasts. These multinucleated cells are mainly responsible for maintaining nutrient exchange and separating the fetus from the mother's immune system.

gancho: A explicação clássica para o bebê humano nascer tão imaturo é o quadril estreito de quem anda em pé. Uma hipótese rival diz que o parto chega quando a mãe atinge o limite de energia que consegue gastar.
explicacao: A ideia clássica tem nome desde 1960, quando o antropólogo Sherwood Washburn cunhou o termo "dilema obstétrico". Andar sobre duas pernas teria estreitado o canal de parto, enquanto o cérebro dos bebês crescia; o meio-termo seria nascer mais cedo e mais imaturo. Os humanos nascem com o cérebro bem menos desenvolvido que outros primatas, e a cabeça do bebê precisa girar para passar. A hipótese foi muito aceita, mas passou a ser criticada. A principal rival é a hipótese da energética da gestação e do crescimento. Estudos com atletas profissionais e com grávidas indicam que há um teto de energia que uma mulher consegue gastar sem prejuízo: cerca de 2,1 vezes o seu metabolismo basal. Por volta dos nove meses, a demanda do feto ultrapassa esse teto, o que coincide com o momento médio do parto; depois, o bebê passa a ser nutrido pelo leite, um jeito mais eficiente de transferir nutrientes. Um estudo da mecânica da corrida também não achou maior custo metabólico ou estrutural em mulheres com pelve mais larga. Ainda assim, há quem aponte outros freios ao alargamento do canal, como o enfraquecimento do assoalho pélvico numa pelve mais larga. A questão continua em debate.

fontes.trecho: This occurs due to the tight fit of the fetal head to the maternal birth canal, which is additionally convoluted, meaning the head and therefore body of the infant must rotate during childbirth in order to fit [...] smaller birth canals in the mothers, and larger brains, and therefore skulls in the babies. Proponents believe bipedal locomotion (the ability to walk upright) decreased the size of the bony parts of the birth canal. [...] and that babies had to be born earlier to fit through the birth canal [...] In addition to bipedal locomotion, the reduced strength of the pelvic floor due to a wider maternal pelvis also leads to fitness detriments in the mother, pressuring the birth canal to remain relatively narrow. This idea was widely accepted when first published in 1960, but has since been criticized by other scientists. [...] The term, obstetrical dilemma, was coined in 1960, by Sherwood Larned Washburn, a prominent early American physical anthropologist [...] Humans are born with an underdeveloped brain; only 25% of their brains are fully developed at birth, as opposed to non-human primates, where the infant is born with 45–50% brain development. [...] The energetics of gestation and growth (EGG) hypothesis offers a direct challenge to the obstetrical dilemma hypothesis, equating the constraints on gestation and parturition to the energy restrictions of the mother. It has been shown in studies using professional athletes and pregnant women, that there is an upper limitation to the amount of energy a woman can produce before it causes deleterious effects: approximately 2.1x their basal metabolic rate. [...] At approximately nine months gestation, the fetus's energy needs surpass the mother's energy limitation, correlating with the average time of birth. The newly born infant can then be sustained on breast milk, which is a more efficient, less energy-demanding mechanism of nutrient transfer between mother and child. [...] Studying the running mechanics of males and females, it was shown that an increased pelvic size related to neither an increased metabolic nor structural demand on a woman.

gancho: Escaneado a cada poucas semanas, de antes da gravidez até dois anos após o parto, o cérebro de uma mãe perdeu massa cinzenta, e a perda persistiu. Para os cientistas, isso pode ser um ajuste fino, como na puberdade.
explicacao: O estudo, do laboratório de Emily Jacobs na Universidade da Califórnia em Santa Bárbara, foi publicado em 2024 na revista Nature Neuroscience e é descrito como o primeiro mapa de um cérebro humano ao longo da gestação. Trabalhos anteriores só comparavam o cérebro antes e depois da gravidez. Aqui, a equipe acompanhou uma única mãe de primeira viagem, com exames a cada poucas semanas. A mudança mais marcante foi a redução do volume de massa cinzenta do córtex, a camada externa e enrugada do cérebro, à medida que a produção de hormônios subia. Segundo os pesquisadores, isso não é necessariamente ruim: pode indicar um refinamento dos circuitos, parecido com o que acontece na puberdade, quando o cérebro fica mais especializado. Também houve aumento da substância branca, que liga regiões do cérebro entre si. Esse aumento foi passageiro: atingiu o pico no segundo trimestre e voltou ao nível anterior perto do parto, um efeito que os exames de antes e depois não conseguiam captar. Como é o caso de uma só pessoa, a equipe está recrutando mais mulheres e seus parceiros. Uma das perguntas em aberto é se o tamanho ou o ritmo dessas mudanças ajuda a prever o risco de depressão pós-parto.

fontes.titulo: New study reveals changes in the brain throughout pregnancy (University of California, 2024)
fontes.trecho: September 19, 2024 [...] Researchers in Professor Emily Jacobs’ lab at UC Santa Barbara have shed light on this understudied area with the first-ever map of a human brain over the course of pregnancy. “We wanted to look at the trajectory of brain changes specifically within the gestational window,” said Laura Pritschet, lead author of a paper just published in Nature Neuroscience. Previous studies had taken snapshots of the brain before and after pregnancy [...] Following one first-time mother, the researchers scanned her brain every few weeks, starting before pregnancy and continuing through two years postpartum. [...] The most pronounced changes the scientists found as they imaged the subject’s brain over time was a decrease in cortical gray matter volume, the wrinkly outer part of the brain. Gray matter volume decreased as hormone production ramped up during pregnancy. However, a decrease in gray matter volume is not necessarily a bad thing, the scientists emphasized. This change could indicate a “fine-tuning” of brain circuits, not unlike what happens to all young adults as they transition through puberty and their brains become more specialized. [...] the researchers found prominent increases in white matter, located deeper in the brain and generally responsible for facilitating communication between brain regions. While the decrease in gray matter persisted long after giving birth, the increase in white matter was transient, peaking in the second trimester and returning to pre-pregnancy levels around the time of birth. This type of effect had never been captured previously with before-and-after scans [...] understand whether the magnitude or pace of these brain changes hold clues about a woman’s risk for postpartum depression [...] More women and their partners are being enrolled

gancho: Um estudo de 2023 apontou a causa do enjoo da gravidez: o GDF15, hormônio feito pelo feto. Mulheres com uma doença hereditária do sangue que as deixa com esse hormônio alto antes de engravidar quase não enjoam.
explicacao: Náuseas e vômitos afetam até sete em cada dez gestações. Em uma a três de cada 100, o quadro é grave, a hiperêmese gravídica, que é a causa mais comum de internação de grávidas no primeiro trimestre. O estudo, liderado pela Universidade de Cambridge e publicado na revista Nature em dezembro de 2023, mostrou que a intensidade do enjoo depende de duas coisas: quanto GDF15 a parte fetal da placenta lança no sangue da mãe e quão sensível ela é ao efeito nauseante do hormônio. Fora da gravidez, o GDF15 existe em níveis baixos em todos os tecidos, e a sensibilidade depende de quanto a mulher já estava exposta a ele antes: quem tem níveis naturalmente baixos corre mais risco de enjoo forte. Uma variante genética rara que aumenta muito o risco de hiperêmese está ligada a níveis menores do hormônio fora da gravidez. No outro extremo, mulheres com beta-talassemia, doença hereditária do sangue que mantém o GDF15 muito alto, têm pouca ou nenhuma náusea. Em camundongos, uma dose alta e súbita do hormônio tirou o apetite, mas não nos que antes receberam uma forma de longa duração. A aposta dos pesquisadores é criar tolerância antes da gravidez ou bloquear o receptor do hormônio no cérebro da mãe.

fontes.titulo: Why seven in ten women experience pregnancy sickness (University of Cambridge, 2023)
fontes.trecho: 13 December 2023 [...] The culprit is a hormone produced by the fetus – a protein known as GDF15. But how sick the mother feels depends on a combination of how much of the hormone is produced by the fetus and how much exposure the mother had to this hormone before becoming pregnant. The discovery, published today in Nature, points to a potential way to prevent pregnancy sickness by exposing mothers to GDF15 ahead of pregnancy to build up their resilience. As many as seven in ten pregnancies are affected by nausea and vomiting. In some women – thought to be between one and three in 100 pregnancies – it can be severe [...] So-called hyperemesis gravidarum is the commonest cause of admission to hospital of women in the first three months of pregnancy. [...] A Cambridge-led study [...] The researchers showed that the degree of nausea and vomiting that a woman experiences in pregnancy is directly related to both the amount of GDF15 made by the fetal part of placenta and sent into her bloodstream, and how sensitive she is to the nauseating effect of this hormone. GDF15 is made at low levels in all tissues outside of pregnancy. How sensitive the mother is to the hormone during pregnancy is influenced by how much of it she was exposed to prior to pregnancy – women with normally low levels of GDF15 in blood have a higher risk of developing severe nausea and vomiting in pregnancy. The team found that a rare genetic variant that puts women at a much greater risk of hyperemesis gravidarum was associated with lower levels of the hormone in the blood and tissues outside of pregnancy. Similarly, women with the inherited blood disorder beta thalassemia, which causes them to have naturally very high levels of GDF15 prior to pregnancy, experience little or no nausea or vomiting. [...] preventing GDF15 from accessing its highly specific receptor in the mother’s brain will ultimately form the basis for an effective and safe way of treating this disorder. [...] Mice exposed to acute, high levels of GDF15 showed signs of loss of appetite, suggesting that they were experiencing nausea, but mice treated with a long-acting form of GDF15 did not show similar behaviour when exposed to acute levels of the hormone.

gancho: Existem gêmeos "meio idênticos": vêm de um óvulo fecundado por dois espermatozoides ao mesmo tempo. Têm em comum todo o DNA da mãe, mas só parte do DNA do pai. Até 2019, só dois casos tinham sido relatados.
explicacao: Gêmeos idênticos surgem quando um único óvulo fecundado se divide em dois embriões. Os fraternos vêm de dois óvulos fecundados por dois espermatozoides diferentes e são, geneticamente, como irmãos comuns. Os semi-idênticos, ou sesquizigóticos, seriam um terceiro caminho. A explicação proposta começa com um óvulo fecundado por dois espermatozoides do mesmo homem. Os cromossomos se separam em três linhagens de células. A que só tem material do pai morre; as outras duas, com o mesmo DNA materno e só metade idêntica do paterno, formam um pequeno aglomerado de células que depois se divide em dois. Em 2007, um estudo relatou um par de gêmeos vivos nessa situação: os dois tinham o mesmo conjunto de cromossomos da mãe e conjuntos diferentes do pai, e ambos eram quimeras, um deles um menino XY e o outro uma criança intersexo XX. Em 2019, a equipe de Michael Gabbett e Nicholas Fisk documentou o segundo caso, com evidência molecular: os gêmeos tinham em comum 100% dos cromossomos maternos e 78% da informação genética paterna.

fontes.trecho: Dizygotic (DZ) or fraternal twins [...] Fraternal twins are, essentially, two ordinary siblings who happen to develop in the womb together and who are born at the same time, since they arise from two separate eggs fertilized by two separate sperm, just like ordinary siblings. [...] Monozygotic (MZ) or identical twins occur when a single egg is fertilized to form one zygote (hence, monozygotic) which then divides into two separate embryos. [...] More unusual are semi-identical twins, also known as sesquizygotic. As of 2019, only two cases have been reported. These "half-identical twins" are hypothesized to occur when an ovum is fertilized by two sperm (polyspermy). [...] If the morula then undergoes a twinning event, two embryos will be formed, with different paternal genes but identical maternal genes. In 2007, a study reported a case of a pair of living twins, which shared an identical set of maternal chromosomes, while each having a distinct set of paternal chromosomes, albeit from the same man [...] The twins were both found to be chimeras. One was an intersex XX, and one an XY male. [...] The likely genetic basis of semi-identical twins was reported in 2019 by Michael Gabbett and Nicholas Fisk. In their seminal publication, Gabbett, Fisk and colleagues documented a second case of sesquizygosis and presented molecular evidence of the phenomenon. The reported twins shared 100% of their maternal chromosomes and 78% of their paternal genomic information. The authors presented evidence that two sperm from the same man fertilized an ovum simultaneously. The chromosomes assorted themselves through heterogonesis to form three cell lines. The purely paternal cell line died out due to genomic imprinting lethality, while the other two cell lines, each consisting of the same maternal DNA but only 50% identical paternal DNA, formed a morula which subsequently split into twins.

gancho: Para impedir que a mãe Rh negativo crie anticorpos contra o sangue do bebê, aplica-se nela... anticorpos. A ideia, testada em presos de Sing Sing, quase eliminou dos países ricos uma doença que matava milhares de bebês.
explicacao: Mesmo numa gravidez normal, algumas hemácias do feto passam para o sangue da mãe, e no parto, quando a placenta se descola, sangue do cordão entra na circulação dela. Se a mãe é RhD negativo e o feto é RhD positivo, o sistema imune dela pode criar anticorpos contra o Rh. Na primeira gravidez o efeito costuma ser pequeno, mas, numa seguinte, anticorpos do tipo IgG atravessam a placenta e destroem as hemácias do feto, o que pode matá-lo. O primeiro tratamento, a exsanguineotransfusão, só agia depois que a doença se instalava. Em 1960, Ronald Finn, em Liverpool, propôs prevenir a doença injetando na mãe anticorpos contra o RhD. Em Nova York, William Pollack, John Gorman e Vincent Freda chegaram à mesma ideia e a testaram injetando anticorpos num grupo de presos da penitenciária de Sing Sing. A imunoglobulina anti-D foi aprovada nos EUA e no Reino Unido em 1968 e, em um ano, já tinha sido aplicada em mais de 500 mil mulheres. Ela reduz o risco de a mãe ser sensibilizada de cerca de 16% para menos de 0,1%. A doença, que matava 10 mil bebês por ano nos EUA, foi praticamente erradicada nos países desenvolvidos. O remédio é feito do plasma de doadores com anticorpos anti-D. O australiano James Harrison, um dos primeiros doadores do programa de Nova Gales do Sul, doou 1.173 vezes entre os 18 e os 81 anos.

fontes.trecho: during delivery, the placenta separates from the uterine wall, causing umbilical cord blood to enter the maternal circulation [...] The first treatment for Rh disease was an exchange transfusion invented by Wiener [...] In 1960, Ronald Finn, in Liverpool, England, proposed that the disease might be prevented by injecting the at-risk mother with an antibody against fetal red blood cells (anti-RhD). William Pollack, (an immunologist and protein chemist at Ortho Pharmaceutical Corporation) and John Gorman (blood bank director at Columbia-Presbyterian) with Vincent Freda (an obstetrician at Columbia-Presbyterian Medical Center) came to the same realization in New York City. The three of them determined to prove it by injecting a group of male prisoners at Sing Sing Correctional Facility with antibody provided by Ortho [...] Yet, this could treat the disease only after it took root and did nothing to prevent the disease. [...] RHIG was finally approved in the United Kingdom and the United States in 1968. [...] Within a year, the antibody had been injected with great success into more than 500,000 women. [...] the disease, which once claimed the lives of 10,000 babies yearly in the US, has been virtually eradicated in the developed world.

Even in normal pregnancies, a small number of fetal blood cells enter the maternal bloodstream (fetomaternal hemorrhage). If a mother is RhD negative, but the fetus is RhD positive, the mother's immune system may develop an immune response (develops antibodies) to the unfamiliar RhD antigens from the fetus. [...] Alloimmunization usually has minimal effect on the first such pregnancy, but, in a second such pregnancy, pre-existing maternal RhD IgG antibodies can cross the placenta in enough amounts to damage fetal red blood cells. This condition is called erythroblastosis fetalis and can be fatal to the fetus. [...] The risk that an RhD negative mother can be alloimmunized by a RhD positive fetus can be reduced from approximately 16% to less than 0.1% by the appropriate administration of RhIG. [...] Conventional Rho(D) immune globulin is extracted from human blood plasma.

was an Australian blood donor known as the "Man with the Golden Arm" for his prolific history of donations, 1,173 times between the ages 18 to 81. [...] was one of the founding donors for the New South Wales Rh Program.

gancho: Um estudo que mediu bebês até todos os dias concluiu que eles não crescem aos pouquinhos: passam de 2 a 63 dias sem crescimento mensurável e então dão um salto, às vezes de até um centímetro num dia.
explicacao: Por muito tempo, o crescimento humano foi tratado como um processo contínuo, só com a velocidade mudando ao longo da idade. A antropóloga Michelle Lampl resolveu medir o comprimento de bebês com uma frequência incomum: uns uma vez por semana, outros duas, e três deles todos os dias; eram 31 bebês, 19 meninas e 12 meninos, acompanhados durante os primeiros 21 meses de vida. O resultado, publicado na revista Science em 1992, mostrou outro padrão: o comprimento aumentava em surtos irregulares, de 0,5 a 2,5 cm, separados por intervalos de 2 a 63 dias em que nada mudava. Os autores estimaram que de 90% a 95% do desenvolvimento na primeira infância se passa sem crescimento algum. Lampl chamou a proposta de modelo de saltação e estase: os ossos se alongam de repente, e o bebê pode ganhar até um centímetro num dia, depois de dias ou semanas parado. Em crianças e adolescentes, as pausas duram de semanas a meses. Num trabalho de 2011, ela e um colega associaram o crescimento em comprimento dos bebês a períodos de sono prolongado e a mais cochilos.

fontes.titulo: Saltation and stasis: a model of human growth (Lampl, Veldhuis e Johnson, Science, 1992), resumo na Europe PMC
fontes.trecho: Human growth has been viewed as a continuous process characterized by changing velocity with age. Serial length measurements of normal infants were assessed weekly (n = 10), semiweekly (n = 18), and daily (n = 3) (19 females and 12 males) during their first 21 months. Data show that growth in length occurs by discontinuous, aperiodic saltatory spurts. These bursts were 0.5 to 2.5 centimeters in amplitude during intervals separated by no measurable growth (2 to 63 days duration). These data suggest that 90 to 95 percent of normal development during infancy is growth-free

Lampl discovered that children grow by saltation and stasis, a process characterized by sudden jumps (saltare, Lat) in size abruptly interrupting days of unchanging size. [...] Increasing size was found to occur as bones suddenly elongate and propel a baby’s length and child’s height by as much as a centimeter in one day, after not growing for days to weeks in infancy, and weeks to months among children and adolescents. [...] Lampl, M., Veldhuis, J., & Johnson, M. (1992). Saltation and stasis: a model of human growth. Science, 258(5083), 801–803. [...] Lampl M., Johnson, M.L. (2011). Infant growth in length follows prolonged sleep and increased naps.

gancho: Aos 5 anos, o cérebro de uma criança usa o dobro da glicose do cérebro de um adulto. É também a fase em que o corpo cresce mais devagar, e cientistas ainda debatem por que as duas coisas coincidem.
explicacao: A pesquisa, liderada pelo antropólogo Christopher Kuzawa, da Universidade Northwestern, e publicada em 2014, juntou dados já existentes de dois tipos de exame: PET, que mede o consumo de glicose do cérebro, e ressonância magnética, que mede o volume. Antes, imaginava-se que o peso do cérebro no orçamento do corpo fosse máximo no nascimento, quando ele é maior em relação ao resto do corpo. Os dados mostraram que o consumo de glicose atinge o pico aos 5 anos. Aos 4, o cérebro gasta o equivalente a 66% do que o corpo inteiro usa em repouso, mais de 40% do gasto total de energia. É também a idade em que o crescimento do corpo chega ao mínimo. Segundo os autores, as crianças humanas crescem num ritmo mais típico de um réptil que de um mamífero, e isso liberaria combustível para um cérebro que, nessa fase, tem o maior número de sinapses. A ligação é uma interpretação. Numa carta, o pesquisador John Skoyles propôs outra explicação: o que ligaria o cérebro faminto ao corpo que cresce devagar seria o risco de hipoglicemia provocado pelos músculos, não uma troca de energia. Os autores responderam que quem acompanha o pico do cérebro é a queda no ritmo de crescimento, não a massa muscular.

fontes.titulo: A Long Childhood Feeds the Hungry Human Brain (Northwestern University, 2014)
fontes.trecho: August 25, 2014 [...] A five-year old’s brain is an energy monster. It uses twice as much glucose (the energy that fuels the brain) as that of a full-grown adult, a new study led by Northwestern University anthropologists has found. [...] It shows that energy funneled to the brain dominates the human body’s metabolism early in life and is likely the reason why humans grow at a pace more typical of a reptile than a mammal during childhood. [...] The study is the first to pool existing PET and MRI brain scan data -- which measure glucose uptake and brain volume, respectively -- to show that the ages when the brain gobbles the most resources are also the ages when body growth is slowest. [...] “After a certain age it becomes difficult to guess a toddler or young child’s age by their size,” Kuzawa said. “Instead you have to listen to their speech and watch their behavior. [...] It was previously believed that the brain’s resource burden on the body was largest at birth, when the size of the brain relative to the body is greatest. The researchers found instead that the brain maxes out its glucose use at age 5. At age 4 the brain consumes glucose at a rate comparable to 66 percent of the body’s resting metabolic rate (or more than 40 percent of the body’s total energy expenditure). “The mid-childhood peak in brain costs has to do with the fact that synapses, connections in the brain, max out at this age

fontes.titulo: Skeletal muscle-induced hypoglycemia risk, not life history energy trade-off, links high child brain glucose use to slow body growth (Skoyles, PNAS, 2014), registro na Europe PMC
fontes.trecho: Skeletal muscle-induced hypoglycemia risk, not life history energy trade-off, links high child brain glucose use to slow body growth. [...] Skoyles JR.

fontes.titulo: Reply to Skoyles: Decline in growth rate, not muscle mass, predicts the human childhood peak in brain metabolism (Kuzawa et al., PNAS, 2014), registro na Europe PMC
fontes.trecho: Reply to Skoyles: Decline in growth rate, not muscle mass, predicts the human childhood peak in brain metabolism. [...] Kuzawa CW

gancho: A ideia de que o cérebro fica pronto aos 25 anos nasceu de um palpite, não de um resultado. Um estudo de 2025, com exames de 3.802 pessoas, viu a fiação cerebral seguir em fase adolescente até cerca de 32.
explicacao: A frase "o córtex pré-frontal só amadurece aos 25" circula em redes sociais, aulas e consultórios. É verdade que exames de ressonância mostram essa região, ligada a planejamento e controle de impulsos, ainda se desenvolvendo depois dos 20 anos. Mas o número vem de um palpite do psiquiatra Jay Giedd, do NIMH, ao comentar na revista Time um estudo que acompanhou jovens com ressonâncias repetidas: os exames iam até os 18 ou 20 anos, e ele disse que, se tivesse de escolher um número, provavelmente iria até os 25. Até o psicólogo Laurence Steinberg, muito citado no tema, disse não saber por que se escolheu o 25. Mesmo assim, o número já foi parar em diretrizes de sentença na Escócia, que tratam os menores de 25 como um grupo à parte. Em 2025, uma equipe da Universidade de Cambridge analisou exames de difusão, que mapeiam as conexões do cérebro, de pessoas de zero a noventa anos. Achou quatro grandes pontos de virada, por volta dos nove, 32, 66 e 83 anos. A fase "adolescente", em que a eficiência das conexões aumenta, vai dos nove anos até o início dos trinta, e a virada dos 32 foi a mais forte de todas. Depois vem a fase adulta, estável por cerca de três décadas. São médias de um único estudo: nenhum cérebro vira uma chave numa data marcada.

fontes.titulo: Is 25 Really the Magic Number? (McGill University, Office for Science and Society)
fontes.trecho: Let’s get one thing straight—the frontal lobe, specifically the prefrontal cortex, is indeed the brain’s command center for impulse control, planning, and decision-making. And yes, it’s one of the last regions to mature. MRI studies do show that this area keeps developing into our 20s. [...] You’ve probably heard it before—maybe on TikTok, in a health class, or from your therapist: “The frontal lobe isn’t fully developed until 25.” [...] The “age 25” marker comes from general trends in brain development, not a single definitive study. Even psychologist Larry Steinberg, often cited in these discussions, frames 25 as more of a ballpark than a deadline. [...] In Scotland, sentencing guidelines now treat people under 25 as developmentally distinct

fontes.titulo: Scientists identify five ages of the human brain over a lifetime (University of Cambridge, 2025)
fontes.trecho: Published: 25 November 2025 [...] Four major turning points around ages nine, 32, 66 and 83 create five broad eras of neural wiring over the average human lifespan. [...] compared the brains of 3,802 people between zero and ninety years old using datasets of MRI diffusion scans, which map neural connections by tracking how water molecules move through brain tissue. [...] Childhood brain “topology” runs from birth until a turning point at the age of nine, when it transitions to the adolescent phase – an era that lasts right up to the age of 32, on average. [...] the adolescent era is the only one in which this efficiency is increasing,” said Mousley. These developments peak in the early thirties, on average, which is the “strongest topological turning point” of the entire lifespan say researchers. [...] At age 32, the longest era, that of adulthood, begins. Brain architecture stabilises compared to previous phases – with no major turning points for thirty years.

It originated from the research of neuroscientist Jay Giedd, who, when speaking to Time magazine, speculatively expressed a desire to have continued his studies on brain development, which ended at age 18 to 20 and found the brain still developing at those points, all the way to age 25. [...] Jay N. Giedd, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and researcher at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) [...] He is quoted as saying, "When we started, we thought we'd follow kids until about 18 or 20. If we had to pick a number now, we'd probably go to age 25." [...] Laurence Steinberg is another influential figure in adolescent brain psychology. [...] He would later say in a 2022 article that he was not sure where the "25" number came from in regards to the age of brain maturity, stating, "I honestly don't know why people picked 25.

gancho: Em camundongos, uma peça do sistema imune ajuda a podar conexões do cérebro jovem. Em humanos, variantes do gene dela, o C4, que aumentam sua produção no cérebro elevam um pouco o risco de esquizofrenia.
explicacao: O cérebro de um bebê produz sinapses, as conexões entre neurônios, em excesso, e ao longo da infância elas vão sendo eliminadas: sobrevivem as mais usadas. Na adolescência e no começo da vida adulta, há outra rodada intensa de eliminação em regiões como o córtex pré-frontal, que parece se estender até a terceira década de vida. Em camundongos, quem ajuda a marcar sinapses para remoção é o sistema complemento, um conjunto de proteínas da imunidade inata que normalmente reconhece micróbios e restos de células: a proteína C3 marca sinapses, e a micróglia, a célula de defesa do cérebro, as engole. Um grande estudo genético mostrou que a associação genética mais forte da esquizofrenia, numa região do genoma ligada à imunidade, vem em boa parte de variantes do gene C4: quanto mais uma variante aumenta a produção de C4A no cérebro, maior o risco. O efeito é modesto: entre as variantes comuns, o risco relativo vai de 1,00 a 1,27, ou seja, até cerca de 27% a mais. Nos camundongos, o C4 participou da eliminação de sinapses depois do nascimento. Os autores sugerem que uma poda excessiva pode ajudar a explicar por que pessoas com esquizofrenia têm menos sinapses, e por que a doença costuma aparecer justamente no fim da adolescência ou no início da vida adulta. A ideia ainda é investigada.

fontes.titulo: Schizophrenia risk from complex variation of complement component 4 (Sekar et al., Nature, 2016)
fontes.trecho: Schizophrenia’s strongest genetic association at a population level involves variation in the Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) locus [...] We show here that schizophrenia’s association with the MHC locus arises in substantial part from many structurally diverse alleles of the complement component 4 [...] We found that these alleles promoted widely varying levels of [...] expression and associated with schizophrenia in proportion to their tendency to promote greater expression of [...] In mice, C4 mediated synapse elimination during postnatal development. These results implicate excessive complement activity in the development of schizophrenia and may help explain the reduced numbers of synapses in the brains of individuals affected with schizophrenia. [...] usually manifest late in adolescence or early in adulthood. [...] C4 is a critical component of the classical complement cascade, an innate-immune-system pathway that rapidly recognizes and eliminates pathogens and cellular debris. [...] In humans, adolescence and early adulthood bring extensive elimination of synapses in distributed association regions of cerebral cortex, such as the prefrontal cortex [...] Synapse elimination in human association cortex appears to continue from adolescence into the third decade of life [...] In the developing mouse brain, C3 targets subsets of synapses and is required for synapse elimination by microglia, the principal CNS cells expressing receptors for complement [...] these alleles showed relative risks ranging from 1.00 to 1.27

fontes.titulo: Scientists identify five ages of the human brain over a lifetime (University of Cambridge, 2025)
fontes.trecho: From infancy through childhood, our brains are defined by “network consolidation”, as the wealth of synapses – the connectors between neurons – overproduced in a baby’s brain are whittled down, with the more active ones surviving.

gancho: Um Nobel manteve viva por mais de 20 anos uma cultura de células de coração de embrião de galinha, e a ciência passou a crer que células eram imortais. Em 1961, Hayflick mostrou que não: as normais param de se dividir.
explicacao: Em 1912, no Instituto Rockefeller, o cirurgião Alexis Carrel, premiado com o Nobel naquele ano por outro trabalho, começou a cultivar tecido de coração de embrião de galinha num frasco de vidro de seu próprio projeto. Alimentou a cultura por mais de 20 anos, mais do que vive uma galinha, e o caso virou prova de que as células se multiplicariam sem fim. Ninguém conseguiu repetir o resultado. No Instituto Wistar, Leonard Hayflick notou que suas culturas de células fetais humanas sempre degringolavam por volta da 40ª duplicação. Para descartar contaminação, ele e Paul Moorhead misturaram células masculinas "velhas" com femininas "jovens": depois de 20 duplicações, só restavam as femininas, o que indicava um contador interno nas próprias células. Hoje se sabe que células humanas normais se dividem de 40 a 60 vezes em cultura, e que o limite tem relação com os telômeros, as pontas dos cromossomos, que encurtam a cada divisão. A maioria das células de câncer escapa graças à enzima telomerase, que repõe os telômeros. E Carrel? Hayflick sugeriu que a alimentação diária da cultura levava junto células novas, vivas.

fontes.trecho: The concept of the Hayflick limit was advanced by American anatomist Leonard Hayflick in 1961, at the Wistar Institute in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Hayflick demonstrated that a normal human fetal cell population will divide between 40 and 60 times in cell culture before entering a senescence phase. This finding refuted the contention by Alexis Carrel that normal cells are immortal. [...] Prior to Leonard Hayflick's discovery, it was believed that vertebrate cells had an unlimited potential to replicate. [...] However, other scientists have been unable to replicate Carrel's results [...] Hayflick checked his research notebook and was surprised to find that the atypical cell cultures had all been cultured to approximately their 40th doubling while younger cultures never exhibited the same problems. [...] Hayflick mixed equal numbers of normal human male fibroblasts that had divided many times (cells at the 40th population doubling) with female fibroblasts that had divided fewer times (cells at the 15th population doubling). Unmixed cell populations were kept as controls. After 20 doublings of the mixed culture, only female cells remained. [...] the cessation of normal cell replication was governed by an internal counting mechanism. [...] The Hayflick limit has been found to correlate with the length of the telomeric region at the end of chromosomes. [...] Cellular senescence does not occur in most cancer cells due to expression of an enzyme called telomerase. This enzyme extends telomeres

He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1912 for pioneering vascular suturing techniques. [...] He believed that all cells continued to grow indefinitely, which became a widely accepted view in the early 20th century. In 1912, Carrel began an experiment at the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, where he cultured tissue from an embryonic chicken heart in a stoppered Pyrex flask of his own design. He supplied the culture with nutrients regularly and maintained it for over 20 years, longer than a chicken's normal lifespan. This experiment received significant popular and scientific attention, but it was never successfully replicated. [...] Hayflick suggested that Carrel's daily feeding of nutrients continually introduced new living cells to the culture

gancho: Além dos humanos, algumas baleias dentadas, como a orca, vivem décadas depois de parar de se reproduzir. Entre as orcas, avós que já não têm filhotes aumentam a chance de sobrevivência dos netos.
explicacao: Viver muito além da fase fértil é raro na natureza: o grupo de espécies conhecidas inclui belugas, narvais, orcas, falsas-orcas e baleias-piloto-de-aleta-curta, e estudos recentes acharam indícios de menopausa também em chimpanzés e gorilas selvagens de Uganda, embora isso ainda seja discutido. Para os humanos, a explicação mais discutida é a "hipótese da avó": em vez de seguir tendo filhos, a mulher mais velha ajudaria filhos e netos, que carregam parte dos genes dela. Em 1957, o biólogo George Williams já sugeria que a menopausa poderia ser uma adaptação. Entre os hadza, caçadores-coletores da Tanzânia, avós buscam alimentos que as crianças ainda não conseguem obter sozinhas. As orcas residentes oferecem um teste: os filhotes não se afastam da mãe, e as avós convivem com filhos e netos. Um estudo com essas orcas mostrou que as avós aumentam a sobrevivência dos netos, sobretudo quando já não se reproduzem e nos anos de pouco salmão. Uma análise comparativa concluiu que, nas baleias dentadas, a menopausa surgiu porque as fêmeas passaram a viver mais sem esticar a fase reprodutiva, o mesmo caminho proposto para os humanos. A hipótese, porém, segue em debate.

fontes.trecho: Humans are joined by a limited number of other species in which females live substantially longer than their ability to reproduce. Examples of others include cetaceans: beluga whales, narwhals, orcas, false killer whales and short-finned pilot whales. Research published in 2023 and 2025 showed that wild Ugandan chimpanzees and gorillas, respectively, undergo menopause.

It suggests that by redirecting their energy onto those of their offspring, grandmothers can better ensure the survival of their genes through younger generations. [...] One explanation to this was presented by G.C. Williams who was the first to posit, in 1957, that menopause might be an adaptation. [...] the post-menopausal Hadza women often help their grandchildren by foraging for food staples that younger children are inefficient at acquiring successfully.

fontes.titulo: Postreproductive killer whale grandmothers improve the survival of their grandoffspring (Nattrass et al., PNAS, 2019)
fontes.trecho: We show that grandmothers increase the survival of their grandoffspring, and these effects are greatest when grandmothers are no longer reproducing. These findings can help explain why killer whales have evolved the longest postreproductive life span of all nonhuman animals. [...] The benefits postreproductive grandmothers provide to their grandoffspring are shown to be most important in difficult times where the salmon abundance is low to moderate. [...] offspring do not disperse away from their mother [...] This results in a close-knit family-based society, where grandmothers regularly group with both their offspring and their maternal grandoffspring.

fontes.titulo: The evolution of menopause in toothed whales (Ellis et al., Nature, 2024)
fontes.trecho: Toothed whales are the only mammal taxon in which menopause has evolved several times [...] We find that menopause evolved in toothed whales by females extending their lifespan without increasing their reproductive lifespan [...] the same pathway that led to menopause in humans can also explain the evolution of menopause in toothed whales.

gancho: Num artigo de 1891, um médico darwinista contou ter pendurado mais de 60 bebês com menos de um mês num dedo ou num bastão fino: só dois não aguentaram o próprio peso por 10 segundos, e um ficou 2 min 35 s.
explicacao: O inglês Louis Robinson era evolucionista convicto, e o artigo em que publicou os resultados, em 1891, se chamava "Darwinism in the nursery", darwinismo no berçário. Em pelo menos metade dos casos, o teste foi feito na primeira hora de vida. O que ele explorava é o reflexo de preensão palmar: ao tocar a palma da mão do bebê, os dedos se fecham sozinhos. Um feto já o mostra até a 28ª semana de gestação (às vezes já na 16ª), e o reflexo some entre os dois e os seis meses de vida. Ele é bem mais frequente em primatas cujos filhotes viajam agarrados ao pelo da mãe, e por isso é visto como um vestígio nos humanos, embora a função seja debatida. Ele parece ser comandado pela medula espinhal, já que aparece até em bebês anencéfalos. O que o faz sumir é o amadurecimento dos lobos frontais, que passam a suprimi-lo. Daí um detalhe curioso: em adultos com lesões cerebrais ou certas demências, esses reflexos podem voltar, e os médicos os usam como sinal de que o lobo frontal está falhando. Hoje, o reflexo faz parte do exame neurológico do recém-nascido.

fontes.titulo: Darwinism in the Nursery (Louis Robinson; Popular Science Monthly, vol. 40, março de 1892), no Wikisource
fontes.trecho: I have now records of upward of sixty cases in which the children were under a month old, and in at least half of these the experiment was tried within an hour of birth. [...] In every instance, with only two exceptions, the child was able to hang on to the finger or a small stick three quarters of an inch in diameter by its hands, like an acrobat from a horizontal bar, and sustain the whole weight of its body for at least ten seconds. [...] and one infant of three weeks old for two minutes thirty-five seconds!

fontes.titulo: Grasp response (Lancaster Glossary of Child Development, Lancaster University)
fontes.trecho: Both grasp response can be elicited in anencephalic infants [...] Such a finding supports the contention that palmar and plantar responses in the newborn are mediate by mechanisms at the spinal level [...] Whether these responses and other so-called reflexes continue to have functions in human development is matter of debate, with one view treating them as phylogenetic vestiges. [...] It was the avid Darwinist Louis Robinson (1857-????) who first described in 1891 that the human newborn was able to support its own weight when holding on to a horizontal rod. Testing 60 infants under one month-of-age, he reported they could maintain the grasp for at least 10 seconds, with one infant doing so for 2 minutes and 35 seconds. See Robinson, L. Darwinism in the nursery.

When an object, such as an adult finger, is placed in an infant's palm, the infant's fingers reflexively grasp the object. [...] A fetus exhibits the reflex in utero by 28 weeks into gestation (sometimes, as early as 16 weeks), and persists until development of rudimentary fine motor skills between two and six months of age. [...] Biologists have found that the reflex is significantly more frequent in infants of fur carrying primate species. [...] This suggests that the grasping reflex is vestigial in humans and in other non-fur carrying primates. [...] That is why the elicitation of this grasp reflex is part of neurological examinations for newborns.

These reflexes are suppressed by the development of the frontal lobes as a child transitions normally into child development. [...] Primitive reflexes are primarily tested with suspected brain injury or some dementias such as Parkinson's disease for the purpose of assessing frontal lobe functioning. If they are not being suppressed properly they are called frontal release signs.
An ardent evolutionist, he helped pioneer modern child medicine during the later Victorian era

gancho: Em um século, as sul-coreanas ficaram 20 cm mais altas, em média. E os holandeses, conhecidos no século XIX pela baixa estatura, viraram o povo mais alto do mundo: 182,5 cm entre os homens nascidos em 1996.
explicacao: Os números vêm de um estudo internacional que reuniu medidas de mais de 18,6 milhões de pessoas para estimar a altura média dos nascidos entre 1896 e 1996 em 200 países. Os maiores ganhos foram das mulheres da Coreia do Sul, 20,2 cm, e dos homens do Irã, 16,5 cm. Em parte da África subsaariana e do sul da Ásia, quase nada mudou. Há um século, as mais baixas eram as guatemaltecas nascidas em 1896, com 140,3 cm, a altura de uma menina bem nutrida de 10 anos. Os holandeses mostram como o ambiente pesa: entre 1830 e 1857, a altura média deles caiu, mesmo com a economia crescendo, e nas cidades, onde se morria mais, a queda foi maior. No fim do século XIX, o país era conhecido pela população baixa. Genes explicam parte das diferenças, mas a maior parte vem de outras causas, como desnutrição e doenças na infância e na adolescência. Um exemplo: crianças maias refugiadas nos Estados Unidos ficaram, em 2000, 10 cm mais altas que as da Guatemala. Já os americanos, entre os mais altos há um século, foram os primeiros a ver a altura parar de subir.

fontes.titulo: A century of trends in adult human height (NCD Risk Factor Collaboration, eLife, 2016)
fontes.trecho: We reanalysed 1472 population-based studies, with measurement of height on more than 18.6 million participants to estimate mean height for people born between 1896 and 1996 in 200 countries. The largest gain in adult height over the past century has occurred in South Korean women and Iranian men, who became 20.2 cm (95% credible interval 17.5–22.7) and 16.5 cm (13.3–19.7) taller, respectively. In contrast, there was little change in adult height in some sub-Saharan African countries and in South Asia over the century of analysis. The tallest people over these 100 years are men born in the Netherlands in the last quarter of 20th century, whose average heights surpassed 182.5 cm, and the shortest were women born in Guatemala in 1896 (140.3 cm; 135.8–144.8). [...] This may be partly due to genetics, but most differences in height between countries have other causes. For example, children and adolescents who are malnourished, or who suffer from serious diseases, will generally be shorter as adults. [...] the same as a well-nourished 10-year girl. [...] The earliest of these occurred in the USA, which was one of the tallest nations a century a

From 1830 to 1857, the average height of a Dutch person decreased, even while Dutch real GNP per capita was growing at an average rate of more than 0.5% per year. The worst decline was in urban areas [...] Urban mortality was also much higher than in rural regions. [...] In the late nineteenth century, the Netherlands was a land renowned for its short population [...] Maya refugees, who ranged from six to twelve years old, were significantly taller than their Guatemalan counterparts. By 2000, the American Maya were 10.24 centimetres (4.0 in) taller than the Guatemalan Maya

gancho: Em 2010, Tóquio foi homenagear seu homem mais velho e achou um corpo mumificado: ele tinha morrido três décadas antes. Casos assim alimentam a dúvida sobre as "zonas azuis", regiões famosas por seus centenários.
explicacao: Sogen Kato, nascido em 1899, era tido como o homem mais velho de Tóquio. Quando funcionários foram visitá-lo para o Dia do Respeito aos Idosos, a família recusou várias vezes. A polícia entrou e achou o corpo na cama; jornais no quarto sugeriam morte por volta de 1978. Parentes receberam a pensão dele, e um foi condenado por fraude. Um levantamento nacional que se seguiu mostrou que as autoridades não sabiam se 234.354 pessoas com mais de 100 anos ainda estavam vivas; mais de 77 mil delas teriam passado dos 120 anos. As "zonas azuis", como Okinawa, a Sardenha, Icária e Nicoya, foram vendidas como lugares onde o estilo de vida faz viver mais, mas a ideia é contestada. Em Okinawa, os registros de família foram em grande parte destruídos na batalha de 1945 e reconstruídos depois, o que alimenta o debate sobre as idades. Os nascidos lá depois de 1945 não mostram longevidade especial, e em Nicoya os nascidos após 1930 também não. O demógrafo Saul Newman ganhou um Ig Nobel por pesquisas que contestam os dados sobre as pessoas mais velhas do mundo. Defensores do conceito dizem ter validado as idades com registros civis e da Igreja.

fontes.trecho: 22 July 1899 – c. November 1978) was a Japanese man thought to have been Tokyo's oldest man until July 2010, when his mummified corpse was found in his bedroom. It was concluded he had likely died in November 1978, aged 79, and his family had never reported his death. Relatives had rebuffed attempts by ward officials to see Kato in preparations for Respect for the Aged Day later that year [...] A study following the discovery of Kato's remains found that police did not know if 234,354 people over the age of 100 were still alive. [...] One of Kato's relatives was found guilty of fraud; his relatives claimed ¥9,500,000 [...] Newspapers that were found in the room dated back three decades to the Shōwa period, suggesting that Kato's death may have occurred around November 1978. [...] prompted a nationwide investigation, which concluded that police did not know if 234,354 people older than 100 were still alive. More than 77,000 of these people, officials said, would have been older than 120 years old if they were still alive.

The blue zone theory represents a region where some people self-attest to exceptional longevity, which has been variously attributed to lifestyle. [...] Suggested blue zones include Okinawa Prefecture in Japan, Nuoro Province and Bolotana in Sardinia, Italy, the Nicoya Peninsula in Costa Rica, and Icaria, Greece. Based on an absence of scientific evidence, the concept of blue zones is commonly challenged as unproven. Subsequent research contradicted initial claims, such as for Okinawa, which experienced substantial decline in life expectancy during the 21st century, and Nicoya, where people born after 1930 did not have exceptional longevity compared to the broader national population. [...] A 2025 assessment of long-lived populations in Sardinia, Okinawa, Ikaria, and Nicoya cross-checked civil birth and death records, church archives, and genealogical records to minimize false-age claims [...] people born before World War II had many centenarians, whereas those born after 1945 had no evidence for longevity [...] The original Koseki [family register] was largely destroyed during the Battle of Okinawa in 1945 and was later reconstructed by American authorities. This has led to debates about the reliability of Okinawan longevity claims

fontes.titulo: Following a Blue Zone lifestyle is purported to help extend your lifespan. But do the numbers add up? (ANU Reporter)
fontes.trecho: Newman, who completed his Bachelor of Science (Honours) and PhD at ANU, won his Ig Nobel Prize for research debunking data on the world’s oldest people

gancho: Há pessoas de 80 anos ou mais cuja memória se compara à de gente três décadas mais nova. No cérebro desses "superidosos", o córtex não afinou como de costume, e uma região é até mais grossa que a de adultos mais jovens.
explicacao: Desde 2000, pesquisadores da Universidade Northwestern, nos Estados Unidos, acompanham pessoas de 80 anos ou mais com memória excepcional, apelidadas de SuperAgers pelo neurologista Marsel Mesulam. Para entrar no grupo, é preciso lembrar pelo menos 9 de 15 palavras num teste de memória tardia, um desempenho típico de quem tem 50 ou 60 anos. Passaram pelo estudo 290 participantes, e 79 cérebros doados foram examinados após a morte. Nos exames de imagem, o córtex, a camada externa do cérebro, não mostra o afinamento comum da idade, e o córtex cingulado anterior, ligado a decisões, emoção e motivação, é mais espesso que o de adultos mais jovens. Ao microscópio, eles têm mais neurônios de von Economo, associados ao comportamento social, e neurônios maiores numa região essencial à memória, o córtex entorrinal, do que pessoas da mesma idade. Os cientistas viram dois caminhos: alguns não acumulam as placas e emaranhados típicos do Alzheimer, e outros acumulam, mas sem prejuízo aparente. Eles também tendem a ser muito sociáveis. O que causa tudo isso ainda é uma pergunta aberta.

fontes.trecho: For 25 years, scientists at Northwestern Medicine have been studying individuals aged 80 and older — dubbed “SuperAgers” — to better understand what makes them tick. These unique individuals, who show outstanding memory performance at a level consistent with individuals who are at least three decades younger, challenge the long-held belief that cognitive decline is an inevitable part of aging. [...] The term “SuperAger” was coined by Dr. M. Marsel Mesulam [...] Since 2000, a cohort of 290 SuperAger participants has passed through the Mesulam Center’s doors, and the scientists have autopsied 79 donated SuperAger brains. [...] “One is resistance: they don’t make the plaques and tangles. Two is resilience: they make them, but they don’t do anything to their brains.” [...] Exceptional memory performance: SuperAgers score at least 9 out of 15 on a delayed word recall test — on par with individuals in their 50s and 60s. Youthful brain structure: Unlike typically aging brains, SuperAgers show no significant thinning of their cortex — the outer layer of the brain — and even have a thicker anterior cingulate cortex than younger adults. This crucial region of the brain plays a significant role in integrating information related to decision-making, emotion and motivation. Unique cellular traits: SuperAgers have more von economo neurons, which are specialized cells linked to social behavior, and larger entorhinal neurons, which are critical for memory, than their typically aging peers. Sociability as a common trait: Despite having diverse lifestyles and varying approaches to exercise, SuperAgers tend to be highly social

gancho: Uma única letra trocada no DNA, um C por um T, faz crianças envelhecerem fisicamente de 8 a 10 vezes mais rápido. A proteína defeituosa que resulta disso também aparece em células envelhecidas de pessoas comuns.
explicacao: É a progéria, ou síndrome de Hutchinson-Gilford, descrita em 1886 e de novo em 1897. Ela afeta cerca de 1 em cada 20 milhões de nascimentos. As crianças parecem normais ao nascer; entre os primeiros sinais está a dificuldade de ganhar peso, e depois surgem traços raros fora da velhice, como articulações rígidas. A inteligência fica preservada. A causa só foi achada em 2003: uma mutação pontual no gene LMNA, na posição 1824, onde uma citosina vira timina. O gene fabrica a lamina A, proteína que sustenta o núcleo da célula. Com a troca, sai uma versão encurtada, a progerina, que fica presa à borda do núcleo e o deforma. Os pais de um menino com a doença, a médica Leslie Gordon e o pediatra Scott Berns, criaram uma fundação de pesquisa sobre ela. Em 2020, os EUA aprovaram o lonafarnibe, remédio que ajuda a evitar o acúmulo de progerina. O interesse vai além dos pacientes: células envelhecidas comuns também ativam a produção de progerina, que talvez tenha um papel no envelhecimento normal, e por isso a doença pode dar pistas sobre como todos envelhecemos.

fontes.trecho: The affected gene, known as lamin A (LMNA), makes a protein necessary for holding the cell nucleus together. When this gene mutates, an abnormal form of lamin A protein called progerin is produced. [...] Most children with progeria appear normal at birth and during early infancy. [...] The earliest symptoms may include a failure to thrive [...] stiff joints, hip dislocations, and other symptoms generally absent in the non-elderly population. [...] This poor processing creates an abnormal nuclear morphology [...] Despite looking and aging physically at a rate 8 to 10 times faster than normal, children and young adults with progeria have normal-to-above-average intelligence [...] In 2003, the cause of progeria was discovered to be a point mutation in position 1824 of the LMNA gene, which replaces a cytosine with thymine.
